screening_results.reason: This is an empirical fMRI study using a social-related body perception task probing perception/understanding of self and others. The sample comprises healthy adults (N=30, mean age 26, 15 males/15 females) meeting the age/sample criterion. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps and contrasts (e.g., own body > scrambled, same-sex other > scrambled, opposite-sex other > scrambled), thresholded and cluster-corrected, with tables/figures and coordinate reporting. Results for the healthy control participants are reported separately for males and females and in combined analyses, satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, age out of range, or missing healthy-group whole-brain maps) apply. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

This study reports task-based fMRI of social processing (understanding others' regret) in healthy adult participants (two samples of 24 adults, ages within 18–65). It uses whole-brain, voxelwise analyses (SPM) with group-level contrasts and conjunctions (IP−IF and OP−OF) and reports thresholded statistical maps and activation coordinates; results are described for the healthy/control group. The task is explicitly social (perception/understanding of others' emotional states). Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusion criteria.

The paper reports a task-based fMRI study using an ecological social-cognition language task (listening to film excerpts and inferring characters’ mental states), meeting the social-related processing objective. A healthy adult group (n=28; inclusion ages 18–65 per methods) is reported and analyzed separately. The authors present group-level whole-brain voxelwise results for the healthy controls (INT>HIN contrast) with FWE-corrected statistical maps, coordinates, figures (Fig.1, Table 2), and detailed methods. Reproducibility analyses for the healthy group are also provided. The study does not rely solely on ROIs or connectivity/resting-state analyses and the clinical group’s data do not preclude the separate healthy-group whole-brain results. Thus it satisfies all relevant inclusion criteria.

Although the study uses fMRI with social tasks and includes a healthy control group aged 50–60, the paper does not report an unmasked, whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map that is clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group alone. The manuscript mainly reports ROI analyses and whole-brain maps for the combined sample (whole group) and group contrasts; whole-brain results provided appear to be either for the whole sample or for between-group contrasts rather than an unthresholded/whole-brain healthy-group task effect. This violates inclusion criterion I5 and meets exclusion criterion E4.

This article is a non-empirical review (in Japanese) summarizing functional neuroimaging approaches and findings rather than reporting original fMRI data from healthy adult participants. It does not present group-level, whole-brain task-evoked statistical maps or original healthy-subject results. Therefore it meets exclusion criterion E6 (non-empirical paper) and does not satisfy the inclusion criteria required for this review.

This study uses task fMRI with a social incentive delay paradigm and includes a healthy adult control group (24 HCs aged 19–36), satisfying I3 and I4. However, it does not provide an unmasked, whole-brain, task-evoked statistical map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group. The reported whole-brain results are primarily between-group contrasts/interactions (BPD>HC, HC>BPD) and ROI-based findings (amygdala), and the authors explicitly state there were no suprathreshold whole-brain activations in the HCs for several contrasts. Because the paper reports mainly between-group contrasts without an accompanying whole-brain healthy-group task effect, it violates the review’s requirement for a healthy-group whole-brain map (E4). Therefore the study must be excluded.

This article reports original fMRI experiments that examine social-related processing (gaze processing, biological motion, dynamic facial emotion) and includes a healthy adult (neurotypical) participant group. The paper provides group-level, whole-brain random-effects activation maps/contrasts for the neurologically normal participants (e.g., figures and descriptions of incongruent>congruent and biological>nonbiological effects), and these healthy-group results are reported separately from clinical groups. Results are presented as whole-brain analyses (random effects) and shown in figures and described in text. Therefore it satisfies fMRI social-task (I3), healthy adult sample reported (I4), whole-brain healthy-group task-evoked maps (I5), and acceptable reporting formats (I6). No exclusion criteria (E2–E6) are met.

This study used task-based fMRI to measure neural responses to dynamic social interactions (dyads) in healthy adult participants (N=21, ages 18–35). Group-level whole-brain analyses are described: whole-brain beta maps were generated, whole-brain contrasts were used for localizer ROI definition (interaction > scrambled interaction, bodies > objects, faces > objects, mentalizing > pain), and a whole-brain searchlight analysis was performed and reported. Results include group-level statistical outcomes and descriptions of whole-brain searchlight peaks. Thus the paper meets the requirements for task-based fMRI of social processing in healthy adults and reports group-level whole-brain task-evoked analyses (reported in main text and supplementary materials).

This is an fMRI investigation of social-related processing (intimacy, empathy, perspective taking toward Self/Loved-one/Stranger). Sample: 36 healthy adult participants (mean age 23), within 18–65. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain random-effects voxelwise analyses (Pain vs Neutral contrasts across perspectives) with voxelwise thresholds and tables of coordinates (FDR-corrected maps and coordinate tables/supplementary tables). Whole-brain correlation and PPI analyses are reported but do not preclude whole-brain task activation maps. Therefore all inclusion criteria are satisfied and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an fMRI study of social interaction perception in healthy adult participants (ages 18–34 across experiments). The paper reports group-level whole-brain analyses (surface-based random effects group analysis and whole-brain contrasts with FDR correction) identifying pSTS clusters for interaction > non-interaction, satisfying whole-brain reporting. The tasks probe social-related processing (perception/understanding of others) using task-evoked fMRI. All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

The paper title and bibliographic details indicate an fMRI study of self-knowledge (a form of perception/understanding of self), which falls under social-related processing. The authors (Lieberman et al.) and the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology suggest a typical healthy adult sample and task-based fMRI design. Given the publication norms and the journal, it is reasonable to infer that group-level, whole-brain task-evoked activations are reported (i.e., voxelwise contrasts) and likely presented in tables/figures, fulfilling the requirement that whole-brain results be available. Therefore the study appears to meet inclusion criteria for: I3 (social-related fMRI task), I4 (healthy adult participants), I5 (group-level whole-brain results), and I6 (whole-brain results likely reported in tables/figures). Confidence is moderate because the provided full-text content was not accessible in this prompt, so the inference is based on title, authorship, and journal context rather than direct inspection of methods/results.

This is an fMRI study of social processing (learning about others’ preference similarity to self) in healthy adults (n=25, mean age 25.1). The task is social (affiliation, perception/understanding of others), and the paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked results (multiple contrasts, conjunctions, cluster-corrected activations with MNI coordinates) rather than ROI-only or connectivity-only analyses. Whole-brain results are clearly described in the text and tables/figures. Participants fall within the 18–65 range and healthy-group analyses are reported separately. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-adult sample) apply. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

This paper reports an fMRI study of social decision-making in healthy adult participants (neuroimaging cohort: n=62 after exclusions; ages 18–53). The task manipulates social information (Locations, Points, Both, Isolated) and examines neural responses to social vs. reward-based influences. The manuscript describes whole-brain, group-level voxelwise GLM analyses (SPM8, random-effects) with multiple-comparisons correction via SnPM and thresholded statistical maps; statistical maps are shared on NeuroVault. Thus it meets the fMRI social-task, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain reporting requirements.

This is an fMRI study of social perception (perceiving person interactions), involving a social-related task (sex-categorization while viewing congruent/incongruent person dyads), conducted in healthy adult participants (n=12, ages 21–31). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain GLM analyses and exploratory whole-brain contrasts (voxelwise p<.001, cluster-based p<.05) with tables of peak coordinates and figures, clearly attributable to the healthy/control group. Thus it satisfies inclusion criteria for task fMRI of social processing in healthy adults and reports whole-brain results.

This is an fMRI study that directly investigates social-emotional processing (schadenfreude and fremdscham) using task-based functional MRI in healthy adult participants (N=34, ages 19–31). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation contrasts (SIT vs NEUT) with family-wise-error (FWE) whole-brain correction and provides coordinates and ROI-corrected results; parametric and connectivity analyses are also detailed. Results for the healthy/control group are reported explicitly (between-group design but healthy-group effects and within-group contrasts are presented). Thus the study meets the review’s requirements for social-related fMRI, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain group-level task-evoked results.

The study used task-based fMRI assessing social cognition (affective ToM, emotion recognition, neutral face processing) fulfilling the social-related task requirement. The sample includes a separate healthy adult control group (18 male controls) reported separately from the psychopathy group. The paper reports group-level task activation for the healthy controls (task-associated activation in bilateral STS and inferior prefrontal gyrus) from whole-brain analyses (whole-brain thresholding described; supplementary tables referenced), satisfying the requirement for a healthy-group whole-brain task effect. Results are reported in text and supplementary materials. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) apply based on the full text provided.

This fMRI study uses a social-related task (participant-generated autobiographical social situations and negative self-beliefs) addressing perception/understanding of self and social processing. The sample is healthy adults (N=35, age range 22.6–55.4), meeting the 18–65 requirement. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked voxelwise contrasts (react vs neutral; reappraisal vs react; acceptance vs react; direct contrasts) with tables/figures and ROI analyses; whole-brain results and coordinates are clearly presented. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-eligible age range) apply. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis objective.

The paper reports task-based fMRI during a faces-versus-houses task (socially relevant face perception), in a healthy adult sample (N=57 total; fMRI subset N=22; mean age ~18.9). The authors performed group-level, whole-brain second-level GLM analyses and report significant whole-brain activations and clusters (bilateral fusiform gyrus; suprathreshold voxel counts and cluster tables/figures), satisfying the requirement for healthy-group voxelwise task-evoked maps. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-healthy-only, pediatric-only, or non-empirical) are violated.

This paper reports an fMRI study using a social-content valence classification task (agency vs. communion), satisfying the review’s focus on social-related processing. Sample: 42 healthy adult participants (ages 18–25), meeting the adult healthy sample requirement. Whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses were conducted using SPM8 with AlphaSim correction; conjunction and contrast maps (agency vs. fixation, communion vs. fixation, and direct contrasts) are reported and described (tables/figures of coordinates referenced). Thus the study provides qualifying whole-brain task activation maps for the healthy group. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity/resting-state-only, between-group-only contrasts, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) are met. Therefore I include the study.

This study reports an fMRI experiment in healthy adult participants (N=29, ages 18–24) investigating communicative speech production, a social communication task involving perception and understanding of others. The paper presents group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (communication vs description, task vs control) with statistical thresholds and tables/figures of activated cortical areas and peak coordinates. Results are reported for the healthy/control group and include whole-brain analyses rather than ROI-only or connectivity-only approaches. Thus it meets the review objective and satisfies the required reporting and sample criteria.

This paper reports an fMRI study of social interaction (free online imitation), meeting the review objective. Participants were healthy adults (23 right-handed females, age 18–30). Group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked activation contrasts are reported (e.g., imitating vs rest, being imitated vs rest, observation vs rest) with correction for multiple comparisons (FWE p<0.05) and coordinates/tables provided. The study therefore provides whole-brain evidence for the healthy group rather than only ROI or connectivity-only results (although PPI is also reported). All inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6 are satisfied and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study is an fMRI experiment investigating social interaction and self-involvement using virtual characters (social communication and perception of self/others). The sample comprises healthy adult participants (18 right-handed males, mean age 25.9; analyses reported for n=17), within the 18–65 range. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain random-effects voxelwise analyses (SPM2) with reported stereotactic coordinates, tables and figures of main effects and interactions (e.g., SOC>ARB, ME>OTHER), satisfying whole-brain evidence requirements. Results for the healthy/control group are clearly presented. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study is not a task-based fMRI investigation of social processing in healthy adults. It uses resting-state fMRI and structural MRI to classify ASD versus controls (multimodal classification), with no task-evoked, group-level whole-brain activation maps reported for a healthy adult group. Participants include ASD and control subjects with a median age of 14.7 years (many under 18), and results are presented as classification metrics rather than healthy-group task contrasts. Therefore it violates criteria requiring task-based whole-brain healthy-group activation maps.

The study reports task-based fMRI using social stimuli (traffic awareness videos eliciting socio-cognitive processing), includes healthy adult participants (two groups of right-handed male drivers, ages 19–30), and presents group-level, whole-brain task contrasts (CV vs NV) with whole-brain analyses reported for each group and in the text/figures. Thus it meets social-related fMRI task requirement, healthy adult sample, and the presence of whole-brain group-level activation maps/results (reported in figures and text).

This is an fMRI study of self–other processing (a social-cognition task) that reports whole-brain, group-level task activation maps for the typically developing (healthy) control group (within-group TD contrasts are presented in tables/figures). The study includes a healthy control group of adults (final TD mean age = 27.3) analyzed and reported separately from the ASD group. Whole-brain results for the control group are reported (within-group self vs. letter and other vs. letter contrasts), and results are presented in tables/figures. Therefore the study meets the review inclusion criteria for (I3) social-related fMRI task, (I4) healthy adult/control group reported separately, (I5) whole-brain group-level task-evoked maps for the healthy group, and (I6) allowable reporting formats. Note: sample includes some adolescents in initial recruitment, but the TD group results are presented separately and the final TD mean age is in the adult range.

This study uses resting-state fMRI and graph-theory connectivity analyses (Network Centrality) in bvFTD, stroke, and control groups; it does not employ any task-based (social) fMRI paradigm or report group-level whole-brain task-evoked activation maps for healthy adults. Therefore it fails the review’s critical inclusion criteria (I3 and I5) and meets exclusion criterion E3 (resting-state analyses only, no healthy-group task activation). Note: a healthy control group is present (I4), but the absence of task-evoked whole-brain results is decisive for exclusion.

This fMRI study uses a social inference task (Why/How) and includes a healthy control group of adults, so it meets I3 and I4. However, the manuscript does not report an unmasked, group-level whole-brain task activation map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group. The whole-brain results focus on a Group × Stimulus interaction and post hoc between-group differences (patient vs control) rather than an accompanying within-group (healthy) whole-brain task effect. Therefore it violates exclusion criterion E4 (reports only between-group contrasts/interactions without an accompanying healthy-group whole-brain task map).

This paper reports task-based fMRI data including multiple social-cognition tasks (false-belief ToM, animacy/intentional triangles, eyes-intention, face trustworthiness, vocalizations), i.e. social-related processing. The sample comprises 78 healthy adults (age range 18–40), satisfying the healthy adult criterion. The manuscript presents group-level, whole-brain random-effects SPM analyses (voxelwise p<0.05 FWE-corrected), figures, and a supplementary table of peak coordinates; maps are also available via NeuroVault/HBP links. These meet the requirement for whole-brain task-evoked healthy-group results and acceptable reporting. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-healthy-only, non-empirical) are met. Therefore the study satisfies I3, I4, I5 and I6.

Although this fMRI study uses a social cognition task and includes a healthy (typically developing) adult control group, the paper reports task-based functional connectivity results (ROI-to-ROI and seed-to-voxel connectivity) rather than group-level, whole-brain task-evoked activation maps for the healthy/control group. The review’s eligibility requires an unmasked, voxelwise task activation map (e.g., main effect or within-group contrast) from the healthy group. Because the paper presents only connectivity analyses without reporting a whole-brain task activation map for the healthy group, it meets exclusion criterion E3.

This fMRI study examines voice-identity processing (speaker vs speech; vocal vs non-vocal sounds), which falls under social communication and perception/understanding of others. It includes healthy adult control groups (n=32; age range around 29–34) reported separately. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked contrasts for controls (e.g., vocal>non-vocal, speaker>speech) with statistical maps/tables of coordinates and whole-brain corrected results described in the text and supplementary materials. Therefore it meets the review’s requirements for a task-based social fMRI study with healthy adult whole-brain activation results.

This is an empirical fMRI study directly investigating social-context vs. non-social episodic memory (social interaction / social scripts) using a task that manipulates social vs. solitary conditions. The sample comprises healthy adult participants (n=24, ages 18–28). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses were performed and reported (SPM5, voxelwise contrasts, thresholding, cluster correction) with tables/figures of activations. Thus it meets all inclusion criteria for task-based fMRI of social processing in healthy adults, and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study in a healthy adult sample (male participants aged 19–60) using a deception task that probes social-cognitive processes (deception/manipulation involves perception/understanding of others). The paper reports group-level, voxelwise whole-brain task contrasts (lie > truth and truth > lie) with statistical maps, thresholding details, tables of activations and figures, and describes small-volume corrections and exploratory whole-brain analyses. All inclusion criteria for the review are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an fMRI study using the Cyberball social-ostracism paradigm (a social-related task tapping affiliation/ social processing) in adult undergraduates (mean age ~19.8). The sample includes a healthy subgroup (37/46 with no Axis I disorders) and reports group-level, whole-brain task contrasts (EX–IN and SUP–EX) with voxelwise results and coordinates. Results for the healthy/group-level effects are clearly described (one-sample t-tests and regression using BFNE), satisfying the requirement for whole-brain, group-level task activation maps. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-18–65 sample, or non-empirical) are violated.

Although the study used task-based fMRI with a social-affective cinematic stimulus and included a healthy adult control group (I3 and I4 satisfied), it does not report any group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical map for the healthy/control group. The paper focuses on dynamic connectivity measures (network cohesion index, NCI) and between-group comparisons of connectivity, without providing an unmasked healthy-group whole-brain activation map or coordinate-based task activation results. Therefore it meets exclusion criterion E3 (connectivity-only analyses without a healthy-group whole-brain task activation map).

This is an empirical fMRI study using a social-related task (self, friend, celebrity trait judgments) in healthy adult participants (n=37, mean age 22.9), and reports group-level whole-brain task-evoked activation contrasts (self vs. celebrity; friend vs. celebrity) with voxelwise statistics (FDR-corrected) and tables of activations. Whole-brain regression and gPPI results are reported and clearly identified as coming from the healthy sample. Thus it satisfies the review’s fMRI task, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain reporting requirements.

This is an fMRI study of social communication/interaction in healthy adults (ages 18–27; final N=29). The task manipulates perceived live versus recorded speech and examines neural responses; authors report group-level whole-brain task contrasts (Live > Social; Social > Standard) with cluster-correction and figures/tables of results. Although ROI/localizer analyses are also reported, whole-brain voxelwise activation maps for the healthy sample are clearly presented and described. No exclusion criteria are violated (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, healthy adult sample, empirical fMRI data). Thus the study meets inclusion criteria for fMRI social-related processing in healthy adults.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants (N=17, mean age 26) that used a social-related task (observation of social vs. individual actions with gaze manipulation). The study reports group-level, whole-brain random-effects analyses, voxelwise contrasts (main effects and interaction) with SPM maps and coordinate tables, satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. The paper therefore meets the review’s criteria for fMRI social-processing tasks in healthy adults and reports whole-brain task-evoked results. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-adult sample, or non-empirical paper) are triggered.

This study reports task-based fMRI of social cognition (affective Theory of Mind, emotion recognition, neutral face processing) in adults and includes a matched healthy control group (mean age ~37.5). The paper provides whole-brain, voxelwise task activation results (e.g., ToM>Emo>neutral main effect and group-by-condition interaction) and reports additional within-group (separate-group) analyses and maps in the supplementary materials. Analyses are whole-brain (not ROI-only) and healthy-control task effects are identifiable in the text/tables/supplement. Thus the paper meets the review’s requirements for fMRI social-task data and healthy adult whole-brain task activation reporting.

This is an empirical fMRI study that directly examines social-related processing (implicit social stimulus processing) in healthy adults. The sample comprises 28 healthy right-handed adults aged 30–50 (within 18–65). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical analyses (ANOVA across the 28 subjects), conjunction and direct contrasts, thresholded and reported with cluster sizes and MNI coordinates, and figures/tables of results. Thus it meets all inclusion criteria for fMRI studies of social-related processing in healthy adults.

This is an fMRI study of social-related processing (recall of self- and other-referential relationship episodes) in healthy adults (final sample n=35). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level task activation contrasts (self-relevant>control, other>control) with cluster inference (FDR-corrected) and tables/figures of significant clusters. Results are clearly reported for the healthy/control group. Reporting includes voxelwise whole-brain analyses and coordinate tables/figures. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-adult sample, or non-empirical) apply. Therefore it meets the review’s inclusion criteria for whole-brain task fMRI in healthy adults.

This fMRI study used social-cognition tasks (attentional and attributional judgements relevant to self), fulfilling social-related task requirement. Participants are described as "normal subjects," indicating a healthy adult group. The paper reports group-level task-evoked activations across whole-brain regions (multiple cortical and subcortical areas named with Brodmann areas), satisfying whole-brain evidence requirements; results are described in text (and likely in tables/figures), acceptable per inclusion guidelines. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only contrasts, non-adult sample, or non-empirical) appear to apply. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for the review objective.

This is an fMRI study using a social judgment/feedback task (social acceptance/rejection), includes a healthy adult control group (n=20, mean age ~28) with results reported separately, and presents whole-brain, voxelwise within-group activation maps for the control group (reported in text/figures and cluster-corrected whole-brain analyses). The paper therefore meets the review’s requirements for task type, sample, and whole-brain healthy-group task-evoked results.

This is an fMRI task study of social-related processing (empathy/theory-of-mind) in healthy adults (N=16 analyzed; mean age 27.8), using a social task (viewing emotional vs. neutral social scenes). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked contrasts (EMOT vs NEUT; TWO vs ONE) with Talairach coordinates, tables, figures and voxelwise statistical maps (FDR q<0.05) clearly attributed to the healthy participant group. Results are not limited to ROI-only, connectivity-only, or patient-group-only contrasts. Thus it satisfies the review inclusion criteria for whole-brain healthy adult fMRI social processing studies.

This is an fMRI study in healthy adult participants (samples: 24 in MDS, 26 in fMRI; ages 22–45) that explicitly investigates social-cognitive processing of political statements (perception/understanding of self/others). The fMRI experiment used task-based whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses (SPM5) reporting parametric effects and thresholding across the whole brain with additional ROI small-volume corrections; results are presented as group-level contrasts and coordinates. Thus the study meets criteria for a social-related fMRI task in healthy adults and reports whole-brain healthy-group task activation maps (coordinates and statistical maps). No exclusion criteria apply.

The study uses fMRI with a social vs. non-social task and includes a healthy adult control group, but it does not report an unmasked, whole-brain (voxelwise) healthy-group task activation map. The main reported healthy-group results are ROI analyses, and the only whole-brain results described are exploratory between-group contrasts (healthy>manic and manic>healthy). Therefore the paper fails to provide the required healthy-group whole-brain task-evoked map (I5) and effectively reports only between-group whole-brain contrasts without an accompanying unmasked healthy-group whole-brain task effect, meeting exclusion criterion E4.

The study reports an fMRI experiment examining interpersonal synchrony and affiliative processing (a social-related task), with behavioral and neuroimaging results. The sample includes healthy adult participants (total N=100 across studies; neuroimaging subgroup reported separately). The manuscript describes involvement of brain areas implicated in social cognition (i.e., task-evoked activation), indicating group-level whole-brain task contrasts/activation maps (reported as regional activations in the neuroimaging study), consistent with whole-brain voxelwise reporting (and acceptable coordinate/table reporting per I6). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-healthy-only, non-empirical) are apparent. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6.

This paper reports task-based fMRI of action observation and weight-discrimination (perception of others’ hand actions), which falls squarely under social-related processing (Perception and Understanding of Others). Healthy adult participants were tested across Experiments 1–4 (total N≈79 healthy subjects) and group-level activation contrasts (e.g., ActionOBS–CtrlOBS; Sleeve/NoSleeve contrasts) are presented. Analyses include voxelwise, group-level statistical maps (reported and visualized across the whole brain and specifically the cerebellum; some contrasts are presented at whole-brain level, e.g., NoSleeve–Sleeve FG4 result). Results for the healthy/control groups are reported separately from patient data. Therefore the study meets the fMRI social-task requirement, includes healthy adults, and provides whole-brain, group-level task activation maps (reported in figures/text/tables), satisfying I3, I4, I5 and I6.

This empirical study used fMRI during an interactive mentalizing task (prisoner’s dilemma) in healthy adults (n=195; fMRI subgroup n=163), directly addressing social-related processing. The paper reports neural activation results described as whole-brain task-related effects (e.g., increased mentalizing-related activity in bilateral temporal poles, precunei, and frontal gyri) and voxel-based morphometry findings, indicating voxelwise, group-level analyses rather than only ROI or connectivity-only results. Thus it satisfies inclusion criteria for task fMRI of social cognition in healthy adults and reports whole-brain group-level maps/results (coordinates/descriptions are provided in text/figures/tables).

This is an fMRI study of social cognition using a social-comparison task (Close Other vs Non-Close Other) performed in healthy adult participants (n=20, mean age 18.7). The paper reports group-level, random-effects second-level voxelwise contrasts (SPM{t} maps) and provides peak coordinates and statistical values for task-evoked activations (reported in text and figures/tables). Whole-group healthy participant results are clearly presented (e.g., Target × Breadth and Valence contrasts), meeting the review objective of fMRI studies of social-related processing in healthy adults. Although multiple-comparison correction was implemented within a priori ROIs, the study presents voxelwise, group-level activation maps and coordinate tables for the healthy/control sample.

This is an empirical fMRI study using a social-cognition task (empathic and forgivability judgments) during BOLD fMRI. The paper includes a healthy adult comparison group (N=14; mean age 30.5) and reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses (SPM99 random-effects models) with coordinates and activation maps/figures for the healthy/control group (within- and between-scan results). Results for the healthy group are presented separately (first- and second-scan activations), satisfying the requirement for an unmasked, whole-brain healthy-group task effect. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, out-of-range ages) apply.

This is an fMRI study that uses social-related tasks (empathic and forgivability judgements), satisfying the review topic. The sample comprises ten volunteers described as study participants (healthy adults), meeting the sample requirement for a healthy adult group. The abstract reports group-level brain activations (e.g., left superior frontal gyrus, orbitofrontal gyrus, precuneus, etc.), indicating whole-brain task-evoked results are reported for the healthy group. Results are described in text/tables (activation loci), so whole-brain evidence is present. Therefore inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6 are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

The study reports an fMRI experiment probing social-related processing: participants judged meaning (social/semantic) versus physical properties of LEGO models, and contrasts probe self/other and collective/individual effects (social cognition constructs). Sample consists of healthy adults (n=25, mean age 24). Analyses report group-level, whole-brain voxelwise GLM results using SPM8 with random-effects second-level tests; results are presented with peak coordinates, tables and figures and corrected thresholds. Thus the paper provides healthy-group, whole-brain task-evoked activations relevant to social processing and satisfies the inclusion criteria below.

This is an empirical fMRI study of vocal versus non-vocal sound processing, which the authors frame as socially relevant (voice processing/social communication). Participants are healthy adults within the 18–65 range (Experiment 1: n=13, ages 21–41; Experiment 2: n=18, ages 18–33). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked activation maps (vocal > non-vocal contrasts) with statistical thresholds described and displayed in figures. Thus it satisfies the social-related fMRI task requirement, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain task results. Resting-state analyses are supplementary and do not prevent inclusion.

This study used fMRI during a social-related task (affiliation and power movie clips) in healthy adult participants (n=17 males, mean age 23.6). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (affiliation > control; power > control) and regression analyses with activation clusters and MNI coordinates presented in Table 1 and Figure 2. These elements satisfy inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, resting-state-only, between-group-only, out-of-range age, or non-empirical) are applicable.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants (ages 19–36) that used a task probing animacy perception from visual motion — a precursor to perception/understanding of others and thus a social-related process. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain random-effects analyses (voxelwise contrasts, FWE-corrected thresholds), figures and tables of results, and ROI and whole-brain MVPA/searchlight results. All inclusion criteria for the review are met and none of the exclusion criteria apply.

This study used resting-state fMRI with instructional manipulations and reports changes in functional connectivity between predefined networks (connectivity/graph analyses). It does not report any group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked activation maps for a social task in the healthy adult group. Although the sample comprises healthy adults (age 18–22), the primary outcomes are resting-state/connectivity results rather than task activation maps, thus violating the requirement for whole-brain task-evoked maps. Therefore it should be excluded under the connectivity/resting-state exclusion.

This is an fMRI study of physician–patient social interactions in healthy adult participants (N=18). However, the imaging results reported here are based on a priori ROI analyses and regression within those ROIs (mOFC/sgACC, rACC/vmPFC, anterior insula, cACC). The paper does not present an unmasked, group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical map for the healthy group (results are restricted to ROI-based inference and FWE correction within ROIs). Therefore it fails to meet the requirement for whole-brain evidence (I5) and falls under exclusion E2 (ROI-only analyses with no whole-brain results). Other inclusion criteria (use of fMRI during a social task and healthy adult sample) are met, but the lack of whole-brain group maps requires exclusion.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants examining processing of mutual vs. averted social gaze (a social-communication/perception task). The sample comprises healthy young adults (reported separately), and the paper reports group-level voxelwise/whole-brain activation maps (t-statistic maps) for the task conditions in the healthy group (in addition to ROI analyses). Thus it meets all required inclusion criteria and violates none of the exclusion criteria.

This study uses fMRI during a social cognition (theory-of-mind) task (Frith–Happé animations), includes a healthy adult control group reported separately (NT controls, ages 19–56), and reports group-level whole-brain task activation analyses (one-sample t-tests and whole-brain contrasts for each group, with results and figures and supplementary whole-brain results). Thus it satisfies the fMRI social-task requirement, healthy adult sample requirement, and the requirement for whole-brain healthy-group task-evoked maps. No exclusion criteria are met.

This is an fMRI study in healthy adult participants (Experiments 1 and 2; mean ages ~20–21, within 18–65) that uses a social interactive task (iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma) contrasted with a non-social control (Gamble), directly addressing social cognition. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps and random-effects contrasts (e.g., PD–Gamble) with thresholding and tables of activations (Figures/Tables and coordinate lists), satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. Results for the healthy/control group are presented (not limited to a narrow subgroup). Therefore it meets inclusion criteria for fMRI social processing in healthy adults.

The study is an fMRI investigation of mentalizing (a social-cognition task related to attachment) in a large sample of healthy adult participants (n=164). The paper reports task-evoked neural activations across the mentalizing network (e.g., precuneus, cingulate, TPJ, IFG, amygdala), indicating whole-brain group-level effects rather than ROI-only or connectivity-only results. Thus it meets the social-related task requirement, includes a healthy adult group, and provides whole-brain task activation results (reported in text/figures/tables). No exclusion criteria are met.

The study includes an appropriate social-related fMRI task (biological motion perception) and healthy adult controls, but the imaging results are presented primarily as ROI-based analyses (STSp and MT localized per subject) with no clear group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map reported for the healthy/control group. Although the authors performed some whole-brain searches, they do not report an unmasked, group-level healthy-task contrast map (e.g., biological>scrambled) suitable for coordinate-based inclusion. Therefore it fails the requirement for whole-brain evidence (I5) and meets exclusion criterion E2.

This is an fMRI study of social cognition (empathy, Theory of Mind, self–other differentiation) using task-based BOLD imaging in healthy adult participants (15 right-handed males aged 18–40). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level random-effects analyses with voxelwise contrasts, cluster thresholds, peak coordinates, conjunctions, and figures/tables describing healthy-group task effects (sad vs neutral; condition contrasts). Thus it meets the review’s requirements for social-related fMRI task, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain task-evoked results. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-adult samples, or non-empirical) are violated.

The study uses task-based fMRI of emotional face discrimination, a social perception task (meets social-related processing). The sample comprises 38 healthy adult volunteers (mean age 27.5), satisfying the healthy adult sample criterion. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked results (FACES>OBJECTS) with SPM maps, tables, and figures (whole-brain thresholding and cluster correction). Results for the healthy group are clearly reported. No exclusion criteria are violated (not ROI-only, not resting-state-only, participants within 18–65, empirical fMRI data). Therefore all inclusion criteria are met.

The study uses fMRI during a social-related task (fearful face processing) and includes healthy adult volunteers, but its analyses focus on functional connectivity using regionally parcellated data and multidimensional scaling rather than reporting a group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked activation map for the healthy/control group. The paper reports connectivity/integration results and between-group connectivity differences, but does not present an unmasked, whole-brain healthy-group task activation map (voxelwise statistical map or coordinate table) required by inclusion criterion I5. Therefore it meets the exclusion criterion for connectivity-only analyses without a healthy-group whole-brain task activation map (E3).

This fMRI study examines facial emotion perception (a social-related process: perception/understanding of others) using a passive viewing task, satisfying the social-task requirement. The sample includes a healthy adult control group (n=27) within the 18–65 age range. The paper reports whole-brain task-evoked analyses (cluster-forming Z>2.3, p<0.05 corrected) and describes within-group activation patterns for face perception; the authors state that the complete list of within-group activations (including controls) is provided in the Supplementary material, and multiple whole-brain between- and within-group results are presented and visualized in figures/tables. Thus the study provides group-level, whole-brain healthy/control task activation maps (acceptable if reported in supplement). No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, out-of-age-range) are violated.

This study reports task-based fMRI during affective and cognitive Theory of Mind (a social cognition task focused on perception/understanding of others). The sample consists of healthy adult participants (n=23) recruited from the general population. The authors conducted voxelwise, whole-brain group-level analyses (contrasts for AToM and CToM vs controls) with cluster-level FDR correction and report results in tables/figures, meeting the requirement for whole-brain task-evoked maps. The design is not ROI-only, not resting-state or connectivity-only, and healthy-group results are clearly presented. Therefore it satisfies the review’s inclusion criteria for fMRI studies of social-related processing in healthy adults.

The study reports task-based BOLD fMRI collected while healthy adult participants (age 18–22) performed a social interaction task (iterated Prisoner’s Dilemma), satisfying the social-related task requirement. Group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses are described (thresholded Z maps and cluster-corrected results reported across sexes and genotypes), with results clearly coming from the healthy sample (OT vs placebo groups). Whole-brain results are presented in figures/tables and discussed in the text. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not resting-state/connectivity-only, includes healthy adults within 18–65, and is an empirical fMRI study).

Although the study uses fMRI during a social-related task (biological motion perception) and includes healthy adult controls for behavioral testing, the paper reports whole-brain task-evoked fMRI results only for a single patient (SL) scanned postoperatively. The manuscript does not present a group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group; comparisons to ‘healthy participants’ reference prior data from other work rather than reported healthy-group maps in this paper. Therefore the key inclusion criterion (I5) for a healthy-group whole-brain task effect is not met. Exclusion criterion E4 (no accompanying unmasked, whole-brain healthy-group task effect) applies.

Although this is a task-based fMRI study of social (mentalizing) processing and includes a healthy adult control group, the paper does not report an unmasked, voxelwise, group-level task activation map for the healthy/control group (e.g., a whole-brain GLM show>no-show map). Analyses are based on spatially constrained ICA component spatial maps and component-level temporal-sorting beta-weights (component-level statistics and group comparisons), not on whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps for the healthy group. Therefore it fails the requirement for a healthy-group whole-brain task activation map and must be excluded (E4).

The study reports fMRI data collected during a live verbal social interaction task (speech/listening/imagination) involving healthy adult participants (22 women, mean age ~27). Group-level, whole-brain voxel-wise second-level analyses (one-tailed t-tests) are reported for talking, listening and imagining, with cluster-thresholding and results presented in text/figures/supplementary tables. The task is clearly social communication-related. Therefore it meets the review’s requirements for task relevance, healthy adult sample, and provision of whole-brain task-evoked maps.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adults (N=20 analyzed; mean age 20.65) that investigates event simulation including social situations and social-cognition processes (mentions theory of mind, trait inference; 41/96 stimuli depict social interactions). The study reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., Imp–Con, Exp–Imp, Ftr–Exp) using SPM random-effects analyses with whole-brain cluster correction and peak coordinates reported; results are clearly from the healthy/control sample. Whole-brain results are presented in text, figures, and coordinate tables. Therefore it meets the inclusion criteria for social-related fMRI task, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain task activation reporting.

This is an empirical fMRI study of social/affiliation processing: participants completed an IAT contrasting "monogamy" vs "adultery" and a go/no-go task with attractive female faces (social/attachment stimuli). Sample: healthy adult males (age range 20–32), meeting the 18–65 criterion. The paper reports whole-brain, group-level task-evoked contrasts (IAT incongruent vs congruent) with voxelwise thresholding and cluster-level FWE correction and provides tables of peak coordinates, satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. Although the go/no-go VLPFC analysis used an a priori anatomical constraint, the presence of whole-brain IAT results fulfills the whole-brain evidence criterion. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, resting-state/seed-only, between-group-only contrasts, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical article) apply. Therefore the study meets the review’s inclusion criteria for fMRI studies of social-related processing in healthy adults.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adults (N=22, ages 18–25) using the DISC stimulus set to probe social attribution (a social-related task). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (FRIENDS > WATCH and FRIENDS > SIZE) with FSL-based one-sample t-tests, permutation testing, TFCE and cluster correction, and describes whole-brain activation results. Thus it meets the fMRI social task requirement, includes a healthy adult sample, and provides whole-brain group-level task-evoked statistical maps/results (reported in text/figures/tables). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, out-of-range age, or non-empirical) are violated.

This is an fMRI study of affective theory-of-mind (social cognition) in healthy adults (n=21 analyzed, mean age ~23.7), using a task involving emotional facial expressions during ToM judgments. The paper reports group-level, within-subject whole-brain task contrasts (EFE > no EFE and whole-brain tables/figures and ROI analyses) clearly identified from the healthy/control sample. Whole-brain results are presented in tables and figures and described in the text. Thus it satisfies the fMRI social-task requirement, healthy adult sample, and provides group-level whole-brain task-evoked statistical maps (tables/figures) meeting inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, out-of-range age) apply.

This study used whole-brain task-based fMRI during passive viewing of social stimuli (social interactions, human faces, erotic images), directly addressing social-related processing. It includes a healthy adult control group (n=14; mean age 28.2) with results reported separately and compares control responses to the social stimuli. Voxelwise whole-brain analyses (repeated-measures ANOVAs) are reported, with tables/figures of clusters and descriptions of within-group (control) activation patterns and simple-effects contrasts, satisfying the requirement for whole-brain healthy-group task-evoked results. The paper is empirical and participants are within the 18–65 range. No exclusion criteria apply.

This fMRI study investigates perception and understanding of others’ actions (anticipation from opponent body kinematics), which falls under social-related processing. Participants are healthy adult badminton players (novice to international), meeting the sample criterion. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain (random-effects) voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., shots–mctrl, thresholded at P<0.05 FWE) with coordinates and figures, and further tables of peak voxels—fulfilling whole-brain reporting requirements. Therefore it satisfies the fMRI social-task, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain result inclusion criteria.

This is an empirical fMRI study of empathy/perspective-taking (perception and understanding of others), using task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (N=23, ages 19–34). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level voxelwise analyses (random-effects contrasts such as Pain > No Pain and target-specific contrasts) with reported statistical thresholds, tables/figures of activation clusters, and PPI connectivity results. Behavioral and dispositional measures for the healthy sample are reported separately. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria are triggered.

This is an fMRI study of legal decision-making that manipulates social-cognitive variables (disgust, trait vs biological personality descriptions) relevant to perception/understanding of others, satisfying the social-related task requirement. The sample comprises healthy adult participants (final N=20, age range 18–45) with analyses reported for the healthy group. The paper reports whole-brain task contrasts and coordinates (whole-brain contrasts, tables of regions/coordinates reported), meeting the whole-brain reporting requirement. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an fMRI study of social-related processing (imagined triadic interactions vs self/other/control), conducted in healthy adult participants (n=19, ages 18–35). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked contrasts (e.g., triad > iron; triad > (self & other)) with whole-brain FWE-corrected thresholds and reports peak coordinates/tables and figures. Results for the healthy control group are clearly reported and not limited to ROI- or connectivity-only analyses. Therefore it meets the review’s requirements for task relevance, sample, and whole-brain reporting.

This is an fMRI study using a social task (modified Cyberball) probing social-evaluative exclusion — directly relevant to social processing. The sample comprises healthy adults (20 men, 20 women; mean age 27.8), within 18–65. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked contrasts (e.g., EX>IN, PG EX>FG IN) with voxelwise FWE correction and provides tables of peak coordinates and cluster sizes. Whole-brain results are clearly presented in text, tables, and figures. No exclusion criteria are violated (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes healthy adult whole-brain task activation maps).

Although the study includes a social perception task using task-related fMRI and reports results for a healthy adult control group, the task-evoked fMRI analysis is reported as an ROI-based analysis (ROI ANOVA) rather than a group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map for the healthy/control group. The paper provides whole-brain voxelwise analyses for resting-state seed-based connectivity (task-free fMRI) but not for task-evoked whole-brain maps. Therefore it fails the requirement for whole-brain task activation reporting and meets exclusion criterion E2 (only ROI analyses with no whole-brain task results).

The study reports an fMRI experiment in which healthy adult participants (N=13, mean age 27.2) passively viewed realistic social interaction video clips (a social-related task). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses are reported (corrected P ≤ 0.05 across the whole brain) with figures and tables of activations (including coordinates and clusters), and contrasts versus rest and versus an ‘alone’ condition. These satisfy the review’s requirements for social task fMRI, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain task-evoked results. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, non-empirical, or out-of-range ages) apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study investigating perception and understanding of others’ actions (force estimation), which falls under social-related processing. The sample comprises healthy adult participants (final N=12; mean age 26), meeting the 18–65 range. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps and contrast analyses using SPM12 (including conjunctions and SUIT cerebellar analyses); results are described with cluster-level statistics and coordinates. The study is not limited to ROI, connectivity-only, or non-empirical approaches. Therefore it meets the review’s inclusion criteria.

This study used task-based fMRI during a social-cognitive/empathy paradigm (dynamic multimodal social stimuli), includes a healthy adult control group (n=24, mean age 35.25) with results reported separately, and presents group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses and within-group T-contrasts (controls) reported in tables/figures (online Tables DS3–5, Fig. DS2) and whole-brain GLM contrasts. Reporting of whole-brain results for the healthy group is explicit. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, resting-state-only, or only between-group contrasts) apply. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants (n=28 naturally-cycling women, ages ~22–24) that used a social perception task (Dynamic Interactive Shape Clips) probing animacy and social relationship attribution. The paper reports whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked analyses (FRIENDS>SIZE, FRIENDS>WATCH, etc.) using permutation testing and cluster correction, and describes group-level whole-brain statistical maps and voxelwise results. Behavioral and fMRI results for the healthy control group are reported separately and in detail. Thus the study meets the requirements for an fMRI social-related task in healthy adults and provides whole-brain group-level activation results reported in the text and figures/supplementary materials.

This is an empirical fMRI study of social communication (real-time mutual eye contact) in healthy adults (mean age ~21.8). It reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (LIVE > REPLAY) with corrected inference and provides tables/figures of activated clusters and interbrain synchronization. Results for the healthy participant group are reported separately and satisfy whole-brain reporting requirements.

This is an fMRI study of co-speech gesture processing during naturalistic narrative comprehension, which falls under social communication/social-related processing. The sample comprises 20 healthy adult participants (ages 22–35). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation contrasts (e.g., low_ID > high_ID; speech > gestures+speech; gestures+speech > speech; interaction effects) with coordinates, cluster extents, tables and figures, and multiple whole-brain statistical thresholds. It is empirical, not ROI-only, not resting-state/ connectivity-only, and reports healthy-group task effects. Therefore it satisfies all inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria apply.

This empirical fMRI study used a social-related task (social attribution/People vs Bumper), includes a healthy adult control group (17 women, ages 18–45), and reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise task activation maps for the control group (People - Bumper group maps and contrasts are shown and described). Whole-brain results are presented in figures and tables and the control group maps are explicitly reported separately from the clinical group. Therefore it meets all required inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis.

This study reports task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (n=29; ages 20–35) performing explicit and implicit facial emotion/age discrimination tasks, which are social-cognitive (perception/understanding of others). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses and SPM random-effects results are reported (FWE-corrected maps and contrasts), satisfying the requirement for whole-brain healthy-group task activation. Whole-brain results are presented in tables/figures and supplemented by ROI analyses. No exclusion criteria apply.

The study reports task-based fMRI collected concurrently with EEG during a social group categorization task (social processing: affiliation/group membership). The sample comprises healthy adult participants (n=20 analyzed; mean age 23.4), meeting the age and health requirements. The paper presents group-level whole-brain task-evoked fMRI results (clusters in mPFC and STS/TPJ) with reported thresholds and coordinates, satisfying whole-brain evidence reporting; results are described in the text and tables/figures. Therefore the study meets all required inclusion criteria for fMRI studies of social-related processing in healthy adults.

This is an empirical fMRI study of social-related processing (self-reference vs reference to others) in healthy adults (n=110, ages 19–31). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain GLM analyses with voxelwise contrasts (e.g., SR>OR, SR+OR>baseline) and FWE-corrected statistical maps and tables, and clearly identifies results from the healthy sample. Although the study also includes effective connectivity analyses (DCM), it additionally provides whole-brain task activation maps. All inclusion criteria are satisfied and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study reports task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (N=30, ages 18–35) using an empathy-for-pain paradigm with experimentally induced (minimal) groups, which is a social cognitive task (perception/understanding of others). Whole-brain, voxelwise group-level analyses are reported (SPM8 repeated-measures ANOVA; main effects and interactions reported with FWE-corrected and uncorrected thresholds and referenced Tables of results), providing unmasked healthy-group task activation maps. Thus it meets the meta-analysis objective and all required inclusion criteria (I3, I4, I5, I6) and does not violate any exclusion criteria.

This NeuroImage fMRI study examines theory-of-mind recruitment during cooperative versus competitive social interactions in healthy adults. The abstract and highlights describe task-evoked BOLD (univariate) analyses as well as multivariate pattern analyses distinguishing cooperation and competition, indicating use of functional MRI during a social task (I3). The paper reports group-level univariate results (ToM regions recruited similarly across contexts), implying whole-brain task-evoked activation maps or voxelwise analyses typical for NeuroImage reports (I5). The population is adult participants (healthy adults) as is standard for this literature and no clinical group is indicated (I4). The manuscript also likely reports results as figures/tables of coordinates consistent with I6. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, or out-of-range age) are apparent from the provided full text.

This fMRI study investigates impression formation (perception and understanding of others), uses a task-based fMRI paradigm in healthy adult participants (20 males, ages 19–31), and reports both ROI and an exploratory whole-brain voxelwise analysis (whole-brain voxelwise ANOVA with results shown in table/figures). Thus it meets the review objective and reports group-level whole-brain task activation maps for the healthy sample.

Study used task-based fMRI during a social interaction paradigm (modified Cyberball) in healthy adult participants (N=15, mean age 24.1). The paper reports both ROI-based MVPA and an exploratory whole-brain searchlight analysis with group-level, whole-brain corrected results (significant STS coordinates reported), satisfying the requirement for whole-brain task-evoked group-level maps. Thus it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, and I5; I6 is also satisfied because whole-brain results are reported as MNI coordinates and described in text.

Although this is an fMRI study of social processing with a healthy control (non-SPD) group, the paper does not report a clear, unmasked whole-brain group-level task activation map identified as coming from the healthy/control group alone. The results mainly present combined-group (SPD + non-SPD) main effects, between-group contrasts/interactions, and ROI/parameter estimate extractions. There is no standalone whole-brain healthy-group task map (within-group control results) presented in the full text; thus the report consists of between-group contrasts and ROI analyses without the required healthy-group whole-brain activation map.

This is an fMRI study of pragmatic language integration (speaker characteristics with sentence content), which is a social-related processing task (meets I3). It includes a separate healthy adult control group (24 adults, ages 18–39) reported separately (meets I4). The paper reports whole-brain random-effects analyses and within-group contrasts for the control group (tables/figures and text describe clusters and MNI coordinates), satisfying the whole-brain evidence requirement (I5,I6). The study also reports ROI analyses but importantly provides unmasked whole-brain task activation maps for the healthy/control group, and does not violate any exclusion criteria. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria.

This is a double-blind, placebo-controlled fMRI study in 55 healthy adult males (mean age ~24.9) that used an explicit social-related task (extended Hariri face/scene matching including erotic/attachment and fearful social scenes), satisfying the social-processing construct. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation results (whole-brain FWE-corrected maps and contrasts are described and shown in figures/tables, with ROI analyses supplementary), clearly coming from the healthy participant group. Reporting includes whole-brain results in the main text and figures (and supplementary material), meeting the acceptable reporting criteria. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-only, includes healthy adults within 18–65, and is empirical). Therefore all inclusion criteria are met.

This is an empirical fMRI study using a social-related task (dynamic happy and fearful facial expressions) engaging perception/understanding of others. It includes a healthy adult control group (n=52; participants in their early 20s, within 18–65). The paper reports group-level whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps and contrasts for both groups (figures and cluster-thresholded Z-statistic images for controls are presented and described), satisfying the requirement for whole-brain healthy-group results. While the study also reports ROI and PPI analyses, these are supplemental to whole-brain activation maps rather than exclusive. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only without healthy-group maps, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) are violated. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

This study reports task-based fMRI during a social communicative/collaborative memory task (directors and matchers), investigating social cognition (mentalizing/theory of mind) and communication. The sample is healthy adults aged 18–33 and group results are reported for the healthy participants. The paper presents group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (e.g., Collaborative > Individual, Individual > Arbitrary, Arbitrary > Individual) with cluster-corrected maps and tables of results; whole-brain ROI analyses are supplementary but whole-brain effects are primary. Thus it satisfies the meta-analysis’ requirements for fMRI of social processing in healthy adults with whole-brain task activation maps.

The study uses task-based fMRI to examine perception of biological motion (point-light walkers), which falls under social-related processing (Perception and Understanding of Others). The sample consists of healthy adult participants (N=13, mean age 28.2), meeting the age and health requirements. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked contrasts (canonical vs. scrambled biological motion) with corrected voxelwise results and provides MNI coordinates and cluster tables/figures. Thus it satisfies the requirement for whole-brain healthy-group task activation maps. Therefore all relevant inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

While this is an fMRI study of a social-related task (irony comprehension) that includes a healthy adult control group, the paper does not present an unmasked, whole-brain, group-level task activation map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group. The manuscript reports main effects across ‘study participants’ (combined sample) and between-group contrasts (controls>patients) and refers to previously published control-group results, but it does not provide a standalone healthy-group whole-brain task map in the text/tables/supplement that can be unambiguously attributed to the healthy group. According to the review criteria, reporting only between-group contrasts without an accompanying healthy-group whole-brain task effect requires exclusion (E4).

This is a task-based dual-fMRI hyperscanning study of social interaction (cooperation/competition) in healthy adults (38 participants, mean age 22.4), meeting the sample requirement. The study uses fMRI during an explicit social-related task and reports group-level, whole-brain spatial maps from group-ICA that are related to task conditions via regression and group-level comparisons (paired t-tests), providing whole-brain task-evoked evidence. Results are presented as spatial component maps and condition-related statistics, and group-level effects for healthy participants are clearly reported. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, resting-state-only, non-healthy sample) are violated.

Although the study uses fMRI during a social face-processing task (dynamic angry/neutral faces) and includes a healthy adult control group, the full text reports only between-group (patient vs control) whole-brain contrasts and group comparisons. The paper does not provide a clear, unmasked whole-brain group-level task activation map or main-effect contrast identified as coming from the healthy/control group alone. Therefore it violates exclusion criterion E4 (reports only between-group contrasts without an accompanying healthy-group whole-brain task effect).

The study is an fMRI experiment involving social communication tasks (viewing, imitating, and producing facial expressions and social hand gestures), indicating social-related processing (I3). The text describes participants (healthy adult participants rather than clinical groups), meeting the sample requirement (I4). The paper reports neural activation locations and condition differences (e.g., IPL and frontal operculum activations and significant differences in locations), indicating group-level whole-brain task-evoked results are reported (I5). Results are clearly described in the text, consistent with acceptable reporting formats (I6). No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only analyses, resting-state only, non-empirical) are evident from the provided information.

Although this is an fMRI study of social-related processing (facial emotion) and includes a healthy adult control group, the paper reports only between-group contrasts and differences (VCFS vs controls) without presenting an unmasked, whole-brain task activation map or within-group (healthy/control) whole-brain results. Inclusion criterion I5 requires a clearly identified healthy-group whole-brain task-evoked statistical map. Because only between-group results are reported, this meets exclusion criterion E4.

This fMRI study used a social-related task (self- and other-reflection), which maps onto perception/understanding of self and others. It included a healthy adult control group (n=21) reported separately. The paper reports within-group, whole-brain voxelwise task activation results for the healthy control group (contrasts self>semantic and other>semantic), with corrected thresholds and descriptions of activations (VMPFC, DMPFC, ACC, PCC, precuneus, etc.), and figures/tables. Whole-brain results are presented (text, figures, supplementary material), not limited to ROIs or connectivity analyses. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria for this meta-analysis.

Although this fMRI study used a healthy adult sample (N=46, ages 18–45) and reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked activation maps (HA− > NTR) and coordinates, the experimental paradigm targets general emotional (negative) picture processing (IAPS) rather than an explicit social-related task (e.g., affiliation/attachment, social communication, mentalizing, or explicit perception/understanding of others). The manuscript focuses on emotion reactivity and fronto-limbic connectivity; while dmPFC has roles in social cognition, the task did not explicitly probe social processes. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I3 (social-related task), and must be excluded despite meeting other inclusion criteria.

This study used event-related fMRI while healthy adult participants (n=16 scanned, 14 included in analysis; ages 18–30) performed a social-evaluative task (trustworthiness judgments vs age judgments). The paper reports group-level, random-effects whole-brain analyses (SPMs), with coordinates and tables of activations (including small-volume corrected results and whole-brain contrasts), and describes task-evoked effects for the healthy control group. Thus it provides whole-brain task activation maps from healthy adults during a social-related task and meets the meta-analysis inclusion criteria.

This is an fMRI study using an action-observation task that examines neural responses to observing others’ risk-taking versus safe actions — a social-cognitive paradigm addressing perception/understanding of others. Participants were healthy adults (undergraduate late adolescents aged 18.0–22.8), within the 18–65 range. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (risk-taking vs safe) using SPM with reported coordinates and statistical maps/figures, and presents results for the healthy/control group. No ROI-only, connectivity-only, resting-state-only, or out-of-range age issues apply. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met.

Although the study uses fMRI with a social-related Theory of Mind task and includes healthy control participants, it does not report an unmasked, whole-brain healthy-group task activation map. The imaging analyses were restricted via small-volume/ROI masks (small-volume correction) rather than reporting whole-brain task-evoked maps, and the reported results are primarily between-group contrasts (ALS > HC) with no clear within-group healthy-control whole-brain activation map presented. Additionally, the healthy control sample includes participants older than 65 (range 35–75) and no separate healthy subgroup aged 18–65 is reported. Therefore the study violates exclusion criteria E2 (ROI-only/no whole-brain results), E4 (reports mainly between-group contrasts without an accompanying unmasked healthy-group task effect), and E5 (healthy sample age outside 18–65 with no appropriate subgroup).

This is an event-related fMRI study of social perception (eye-gaze intention processing), directly addressing social-related processing. The paper reports results for a neurologically normal (control) group separately (n=9, mean age 23.4, range 15.5–32.4) and provides group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise statistical maps and coordinate tables and figures (random-effects analyses, Table 1, and activation maps for the control group). Whole-brain contrasts (incongruent > congruent) for the healthy/control group are explicitly reported. Therefore it meets the fMRI social-task requirement, has a healthy control group with reported group-level results, and provides whole-brain evidence in figures/tables. (Note: control group includes one participant aged 15.5, but group-level healthy adult results are presented and the majority of the group falls within 18–65.)

This fMRI study investigates face emotion discrimination — a social cognition task (perception/understanding of others). The sample is a community-based group of healthy adults screened to exclude Axis I diagnoses, and results include group-level whole-brain task activation analyses (one-sample t-tests across participants and flexible factorial group analyses) reported as tables of coordinates and figures. The paper therefore provides whole-brain, task-evoked maps for healthy adult participants and is not limited to ROI-only or connectivity-only analyses.

This is an empirical fMRI study using a social-related task (empathy toward humans and animals) in healthy adults (ages 18–60). The paper reports whole-brain, voxelwise group-level task contrasts (human > neutral; animal > neutral) analyzed with SPM2 and reports peak coordinates and thresholded results (p<0.05 FWE), plus within-group statistical maps and between-group analyses. Therefore it satisfies all inclusion requirements for whole-brain healthy adult task activation reporting. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, resting-state/connectivity-only, age outside range, or non-empirical) are triggered.

The study appears to be an fMRI experiment on perception of faces (socially relevant stimuli) in healthy adult observers, satisfying the social-processing and healthy-sample requirements. However, the provided full-text summary does not clearly state that any group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation maps were reported for the healthy group. The summary describes activations in specific regions (FFA, STS, amygdala) and correlations, which could reflect ROI-based analyses. Because inclusion criterion I5 (reporting at least one whole-brain voxelwise group task map) cannot be verified from the supplied content, the study must be excluded per review rules. If full text confirms whole-brain group-level voxelwise results (e.g., whole-brain contrasts/activation maps or coordinate tables for group-level effects), it could be reconsidered for inclusion.

This fMRI study tested voice processing—a social-perception task—using whole-brain analyses and reports clear group-level results for a healthy adult control group. The paper includes eight healthy adult volunteers (ages reported, adult range), and reports random-effect, whole-brain activation for the control group (voice vs. non-voice, P < 0.001 corrected) with figures/tables described in the text and supplementary materials. Although the study also includes an autism clinical group, results for the healthy group are reported separately. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, missing healthy-group whole-brain maps, or non-empirical paper) apply. Therefore it meets the review’s inclusion criteria for fMRI studies of social-related processing in healthy adults.

This fMRI study measured neural responses in healthy adult participants (N=18, ages 18–27) while they listened to literary stories and contrasted Mentalizing versus Action content. The design probes social-related processing (mentalizing/theory-of-mind) during a task (story comprehension) and used a Theory-of-Mind localizer to identify mentalizing ROIs. The paper reports group-level whole-brain task contrasts (Mentalizing > Action and Action > Mentalizing) with corrected voxelwise/cluster thresholds and provides cluster locations/activations. Thus the study meets criteria for (I3) social-related fMRI task, (I4) healthy adult sample, (I5) whole-brain group-level task-evoked maps, and (I6) acceptable reporting of whole-brain results.

This is an fMRI study of social gaze-following (a social-related task examining responses to in-group vs. out-group political faces), conducted in healthy adult participants (ages 18–36).
