The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task activation contrasts (e.g., incongruent > congruent) with cluster-level correction and provides tables and figures describing activated clusters across the brain (dorsal and ventral fronto-parietal networks, FEF, parietal, occipital regions). Results are reported for the healthy/control sample (no clinical groups). Thus it satisfies the review inclusion criteria and does not violate any exclusion criteria.

This is an event-related fMRI study of empathy for others' pain (social-related processing: perception/understanding of others). It includes a healthy adult control group (n=13; ages mean 33) reported separately from the congenital insensitivity to pain patients. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task contrasts and tables of coordinates and figures for the control group (within-group activations such as AI, aMCC, insula, etc.), satisfying whole-brain voxelwise reporting. Results are not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, and healthy-group effects are clearly identified. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met.

This is an empirical fMRI study of social cognition (Theory of Mind) using the REMICS task (social vs physical scenarios) in a sample of healthy adults (N=19, ages 20–53). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation contrasts (e.g., SocAdj>PhyConf, Soc>Phy, Adj>Conf) with peak coordinates and tables of significant clusters (voxelwise threshold p<.001, cluster correction), clearly attributed to the healthy/control group. Thus it meets the review inclusion criteria for fMRI social-related task, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain reported results.

The study meets the review topic (fMRI of social/attachment processing) and includes healthy adult participants (women aged 22–45). However, the published analyses and significance testing were conducted using an a priori ROI approach with small-volume correction (SVC), and the paper frames results as ‘regions of interest’ findings. There is no clear report of an unmasked, whole-brain (voxelwise) group-level task activation map or whole-brain corrected results independent of ROIs. Because the paper reports only ROI/SVC-based task results rather than an unmasked whole-brain task map, it fails inclusion criterion I5 and must be excluded under E2.

This is an empirical event-related fMRI study in healthy adults (n=34, ages 20–28) using a theory-of-mind/false-belief social task (perception/understanding of others). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked activation maps and coordinates (random-effects analysis, SPM2; figures and Table 1), and describes thresholds and ROIs; results are clearly from the healthy participant group. The study therefore meets the meta-analysis requirements for fMRI during social-related tasks, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain reporting. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity/resting-state only, between-group-only contrasts, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) are violated.

This fMRI study used a task (listening to and rating artistic vs. popular music) that elicited and analyzed social-cognition/ToM and empathy-related activations. Authors explicitly report greater recruitment of default mode network/ToM and cognitive-empathy regions (arMFC, PCC/PC, TP, hippocampus) for artistic music and interpret these as social-cognitive/empathic processing. The sample is healthy adults (male, 18–24), and group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation results are reported with coordinates/tables and cluster-level corrections. Thus the paper provides whole-brain healthy-group task activation maps relevant to social-related processing and satisfies the review’s inclusion criteria.

This is an fMRI study that directly manipulated social information (trustworthiness judgments) versus nonsocial information during an n-back task. Participants were healthy adults (mean age 22; final imaging N=14), within the 18–65 range. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (2×2 repeated-measures ANOVA) with cluster correction and tables of peak coordinates (Tables 2–4), clearly identifying healthy-group task effects. Thus it meets the review’s requirements for fMRI social-task data, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain task activation reporting. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity/resting-state only, non-healthy-only groups, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) are violated.

The study is an fMRI investigation of empathy for pain (a social/’Perception and Understanding of Others’ task) in healthy adult volunteers. It includes a young healthy subgroup (ages 20–30) satisfying the 18–65 sample requirement, and reports group-level, whole-brain task activation maps (pain>no pain and pain>baseline) with results and statistical maps made available (figures/tables and NeuroVault/supplement). Whole-brain voxelwise analyses (one-sample t-tests and second-level contrasts) are reported rather than only ROI/seed/connectivity results. Therefore it meets the meta-analysis objective and inclusion criteria.

Insufficient information in the provided full text to confirm that the paper reports a healthy adult group with a clearly identified, group-level whole-brain task-evoked activation map. The study title and focus (schizophrenia out-patients) suggest emphasis on patient vs control comparisons and it likely reports between-group contrasts without an unmasked healthy-group task effect. Therefore it does not meet inclusion criteria I4/I5 and matches exclusion criterion E4.

While this fMRI study uses a social (mentalizing) task and includes a healthy adult control group (I3, I4), the paper does not report an unmasked, group-level whole-brain task activation map for the healthy/control group. The manuscript’s whole-brain analysis is reported only as a between-group contrast (Controls > ASC) and the within-group findings are reported primarily via ROI analyses. Therefore it lacks a clearly identified healthy-group whole-brain task effect, violating inclusion criterion I5 and falling under exclusion criterion E4.

This is an fMRI study of social cognition (race perception/trustworthiness), using task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (N=30, ages 18–29). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (e.g., Black>White) and second-level covariate analyses with tables and peak coordinates, and describes PPI connectivity alongside whole-brain results. Thus it meets criteria for a social-related fMRI task, appropriate healthy adult sample, and provides whole-brain task-evoked statistical maps (reported with coordinates).

This study uses task-based fMRI to investigate processing of dynamic emotional facial expressions (a social perception task) and reports whole-brain group-level activation for the healthy/control group (control group simple main effect of dynamic vs static, with corrected whole-brain results and coordinates/figures). The paper includes a separate healthy adult control group (n=13, ages within 18–65) with results reported independently from the ASD group. Whole-brain statistical maps and coordinate tables for the control group are presented. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria and violates no exclusions.

The paper is a short conference abstract that describes dyadic fMRI and network synchronizations but does not report essential information required by the review. There is no information on participant sample characteristics (age range, number of healthy adults), and no presentation of group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical maps for a healthy adult group. The abstract appears focused on methodological development and connectivity/synchronization analyses rather than reporting unmasked whole-brain task activation results. Therefore it does not meet the review's requirements for whole-brain healthy-group task activation reporting.

This study used task-based fMRI of a social judgment (approachability) task (meets social-related construct). It included a healthy adult control group (adults recruited; controls analyzed separately) and reports within-group/whole-brain task contrasts and activations (social > gender and baseline) with group-level voxelwise analyses and supplementary tables/figures for within-group results. Results are not limited to ROI, connectivity, or between-group contrasts only. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, age outside range, or non-empirical) apply.

The paper reports task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (three experiments, N=25, N=65, N=178; Experiment 2 mean age 40.9) using a social cognition paradigm (EmpaToM) probing empathy and Theory of Mind, addressing social-related processing. Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts are reported (e.g., empathy contrast, ToM contrast) with tables of activation peaks and figures; second-level one-sample t-tests and FWE-corrected thresholds are described. Behavioral and imaging results for the healthy/control samples are reported separately. Thus the study meets the meta-analysis requirements for task-based fMRI in healthy adults with whole-brain task activation maps and coordinate tables.

This is an empirical fMRI study of social cognition in healthy adults. It used task-based fMRI during a social/competitive matching-pennies paradigm involving human and non-human agents (social-related processing/mentalizing). The sample comprises healthy adult participants (n=16, ages 18–25). The paper reports whole-brain, voxelwise GLM group-level random-effects analyses with voxelwise thresholding (p<.001) and cluster-level FWE correction across the whole brain; results are presented in figures and tables with coordinates. Thus all inclusion criteria are met (task-based fMRI of social processing, healthy adult sample, whole-brain group-level voxelwise results, and appropriately reported maps/tables). No exclusion criteria apply.

This fMRI study investigates emotion recognition (a social cognitive task) and includes a healthy adult control group, but the full text reports primarily between-group contrasts and ROI results. The paper does not present an unambiguous, whole-brain, group-level task activation map explicitly identified as coming from the healthy/control group (only group comparisons, interactions, and ROI amygdala results are reported). Therefore it fails the requirement to report a healthy-group whole-brain task-evoked statistical map (I5) and meets exclusion criterion E4 (only between-group contrasts/interactions without an accompanying unmasked whole-brain healthy-group task effect).

This empirical fMRI study investigates emotional sentence attribution (a social-cognition task involving emotion processing and theory-of-mind inference) and includes a healthy adult control group (n=25). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (FWE-corrected) for task effects and group × task interactions, and specifically describes/control-related activations (controls significantly activated mPFC during EMO>GRAM). Whole-brain results are presented in figures/tables and described in the text. No exclusion criteria apply. Minor uncertainty (reduced confidence) stems from the excerpt not explicitly listing participant ages, but the sample is described as adult and matched, so I4 is satisfied.

This is an fMRI study of social-related processing (empathic concern for characters in film clips) in healthy adults. The sample comprises 26 healthy adult participants (mean age 30.3), satisfying the age and healthy-sample requirement. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked voxelwise analyses (ANOVA and contrasts, Tables 1–2, and whole-brain figures) and parametric modulation results for the healthy group, which meet the whole-brain evidence criterion; results are presented in text, tables, and figures. The study additionally includes connectivity (DCM), but also reports univariate whole-brain activations, so it does not violate exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only or connectivity-only). Therefore all inclusion criteria are met.

This study reports task-based fMRI during a social-cognition (second-order Theory of Mind) task, includes a healthy adult control group (n=25; ages 18–60) with results reported separately, and presents voxelwise whole-brain analyses and reported activation coordinates (Table 2) and figures. The paper also reports within-group/ROI extractions and correlations for the healthy control group and provides whole-brain statistical maps/figures (e.g., whole-brain analysis images and tables of coordinates). Therefore it meets the review’s requirements for fMRI social task data in healthy adults and reporting of whole-brain healthy-group task effects.

This study used task-based fMRI during a social cognition task (face-based trustworthiness judgments with feedback), includes a healthy younger adult group (ages 20–33) meeting the 18–65 requirement, and reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses (second-level ANOVA and whole-brain results, with tables/figures reporting activations). Whole-brain results are clearly described and reported (ANOVA, contrasts, tables/figures), satisfying reporting requirements. Therefore it meets the meta-analysis inclusion criteria for fMRI studies of social processing in healthy adults.

The study uses fMRI of social processing (racial ingroup/outgroup face perception) in presumably healthy adult participants, but the full text/abstract does not clearly report a group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) task activation map for the healthy/control group. The paper emphasizes an ROI-based analysis of amygdala voxels and does not provide explicit whole-brain voxelwise results or coordinates that can be clearly identified as unmasked healthy-group whole-brain effects. Because inclusion criterion I5 (whole-brain evidence) is not demonstrably met, this study must be excluded per exclusion criterion E2 (studies reporting only ROI analyses with no whole-brain results).

Study uses fMRI of facial emotion processing (social task) and reports within-group whole-brain maps for the healthy control group; however, the participant age range reported is 16–35 and controls were age-matched to that sample. Inclusion criterion I4 requires at least one group of healthy adult participants aged 18–65. Because the healthy/control group includes participants younger than 18 (min age 16) and no adult-only healthy subgroup is reported separately, the study does not meet the age requirement. Therefore it must be excluded under E5.

This is an fMRI study probing emotion processing and mirror neuron responses (social-cognitive constructs: perception/understanding of others/emotion). Sample comprises healthy adults (n=19; mean age 27.7, within 18–65). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., untrained>trained whole-brain cluster-corrected results in SMA and IFG) and includes coordinate/cluster information. Although ROI analyses were also conducted, whole-brain task-evoked maps for the healthy group are clearly presented. No exclusion criteria apply.

This is an fMRI experiment with healthy adult participants (mean age 24.6) using a social task (observed eye contact and gaze-following). The manuscript reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts with statistical thresholds and coordinate tables/figures (e.g., EC > AG, Cong > Incong, interaction contrasts), clearly from the healthy sample. Thus it satisfies the review’s requirements for social-related fMRI activation in healthy adults and meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6. No exclusion criteria are violated.

Although this is an fMRI study of face processing (a social perception task) and includes a healthy adult control group, the neuroimaging analyses are conducted as region-of-interest (individual right FFA) analyses rather than reporting group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical maps for the healthy/control group. The paper localizes individual FFAs and extracts ROI beta weights/amplitudes for between-group and within-group comparisons; no unmasked, group-level whole-brain activation map for the healthy group is provided. Therefore it does not meet the requirement for whole-brain healthy-group task effects and must be excluded.

This study used task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (N=23, ages 19–32) while they read a narrative and provided suspense ratings. The task probes social-cognitive processes (mentalizing/theory-of-mind and inference about characters), and the authors explicitly interpret activations as related to social cognition (MFC, TPJ). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (second-level random effects SPM results) are reported with cluster- and ROI-corrected statistics and tables/figures of coordinates. Thus the paper provides whole-brain task-evoked maps from a healthy adult sample for a social-related process (perception/understanding of others).

This paper is a single-case study (patient PK) with comparisons to control subjects using fMRI during face processing. Although it addresses social-related processing and includes healthy control participants, the full-text/abstract does not report an unmasked, group-level whole-brain task activation map for the healthy/control group. The main reported findings are case-versus-control differences and connectivity analyses (hypoactivation in left aSTS/MTG in the patient; decreased inter-hemispheric connectivity), which appear to be between-group contrasts and connectivity results rather than an explicit healthy-group whole-brain task effect. Therefore it does not meet the requirement for reporting a healthy-group whole-brain task-evoked statistical map (I5) and falls under exclusion criterion E4.

This is an empirical fMRI study that measured emotion processing and theory-of-mind tasks using faces/eyes (social-related tasks) and reports group-level activation maps for healthy adult controls (N=14). Whole-brain voxelwise analyses are presented (within-group contrasts EMOTION–GENDER with thresholding) with figures and supplementary tables describing healthy-group activations. Healthy participants are adults within the 18–65 range and their results are reported separately from patient and sibling groups. No exclusion criteria are met (not ROI-only, not connectivity/resting-state-only, and includes unmasked healthy-group task effects).

This study reports an fMRI task probing social perception (observation of cooperative vs noncooperative interactions), includes a clearly reported healthy adult control group (n=19) analyzed separately, and provides whole-brain, voxelwise group-level task contrasts for the healthy controls (e.g., C+ > C–; FDR- and FWE-corrected results, MNI coordinates reported). The task is social-related (perception/understanding of others), and whole-brain healthy-group activation maps/contrasts are explicitly described. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, resting-state-only, or absence of healthy-group whole-brain task maps) apply. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria for the meta-analysis.

This is an fMRI study that implemented a social-related task (evaluative judgments of guilt and embarrassment; Theory of Mind/social cognition), recruited a healthy adult sample (N=19, ages within 18–65), and reported group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise analyses (random-effects contrasts G−N, E−N, G−E, E−G) with coordinate tables and figures. Whole-brain statistical thresholds and extent criteria are described, and regression analyses with group-level maps are reported. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

The study is an fMRI investigation of empathy and perspective-taking (social cognition), meeting the review’s topic. Participants are healthy adults aged 21–31 (N=18), satisfying the sample criterion. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., Self vs Other, View-Pain vs View-No-Pain) with cluster- and peak-level FWE correction and tables/coordinates, fulfilling whole-brain evidence requirements. Results for the healthy/control group are clearly presented (including conjunction analyses, time-course analyses, and ROI-corrected contrasts), and whole-brain findings are described in text, tables, and figures. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, or out-of-range participants) apply. Therefore all inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6 are met.

This is an empirical fMRI study employing a social-perception task (face discrimination) with intranasal oxytocin. The sample includes a healthy adult control group (n=14; ages ~24) and results for controls are reported separately (ROI and group-specific contrasts). The paper reports group-level voxelwise whole-brain analyses (faces>houses) for the whole sample and follow-up group-level analyses for each group, including coordinates and SVC-corrected clusters identified for the neurotypical control group. Whole-brain results are reported in tables/figures with coordinates. Although some effects used small-volume correction within a face-processing mask, group-level voxelwise task-evoked maps/coordinates for the healthy/control group are clearly presented, satisfying inclusion criteria.

This study used task-based fMRI during social-related processing (thinking about 16 social-interaction items), includes a healthy adult control group (17 age- and IQ-matched controls), and reports group-level within-group whole-brain task contrasts for the control group (all social interactions vs fixation) with associated figures/tables. The healthy participants are adults (young adults) and results for the control group are reported separately from the autism group. Thus it satisfies I3 (fMRI social task), I4 (healthy adult group reported), I5 (whole-brain group-level task-evoked map for controls), and I6 (results presented in text/figures/tables). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only without healthy map, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) apply.

This is an empirical fMRI study using an ecologically valid social interaction task (adapted Taylor Aggression Paradigm) presenting opponents' facial expressions; sample comprises healthy adult males (32 included in analyses, mean age 23.3); the paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked contrasts (angry > neutral) with cluster-wise FWE correction and presents tables/figures of whole-brain results. Thus it satisfies fMRI social processing, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain reporting requirements.

This is an empirical fMRI study examining cross-modal face and voice perception (a social perception/communication task) in a sample of 20 participants, reporting group-level task contrasts that identify brain regions (e.g., hippocampus, occipital and temporal cortices) and analyses of task-evoked connectivity (PPI). The study therefore provides whole-brain, group-level task-evoked activation results from healthy adult participants and addresses social-related processing. All inclusion criteria are met: I3 (social-related fMRI task: face/voice perception), I4 (healthy adult sample reported), I5 (group-level whole-brain task-evoked results reported in the paper), and I6 (results reported as regional activations/contrasts). Confidence is reduced slightly because the brief record does not state exact participant ages or show coordinate tables/figures here, but the abstract and methods summary indicate whole-brain activation reporting in healthy adults.

This is an empirical fMRI study that explicitly probes social-emotional processing (images of group interactions vs individuals) and instructs participants to imagine themselves in the scenarios, matching the social-related constructs. A healthy control group of adults (mean age 32.4) is reported separately. The paper presents group-level, voxelwise task activation results for the control group (main effects and contrasts with reported MNI coordinates and corrected statistical thresholds), satisfying the whole-brain reporting requirement. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria are triggered.

The study used fMRI with a social-emotional face task and reports whole-brain group maps for controls, but all participant groups are adolescents (ages 12–18) with no healthy adult (18–65) subgroup. This violates the age eligibility requirement. Per exclusion criterion E5, studies that include only participants outside age 18–65 are excluded unless a healthy adult subgroup is reported separately. Therefore the study must be excluded.

This is an empirical fMRI study of social communication/influence in healthy adult participants (mean age ~20.6). The task involved social processing (message encoding/intention to recommend) and used task-based whole-brain voxelwise analyses reported at the group level (whole-brain results with MNI coordinates and thresholding are provided). Thus it meets the review’s neuroimaging and sample requirements and reports whole-brain activation maps rather than ROI- or connectivity-only results.

This study reports an fMRI mentalizing paradigm (social-cognitive task) and includes an age- and IQ-matched healthy adult control group (18 adults) alongside an autism spectrum group. The abstract and results describe task-evoked brain activations (e.g., medial prefrontal cortex and temporoparietal junction) tied to the mentalizing paradigm, indicating voxelwise whole-brain fMRI analyses. Thus the paper meets the review’s focus on social-related fMRI processing in healthy adults and provides group-level activation results for the control group (reported in main text/figures). Therefore it satisfies the inclusion requirements for social-related fMRI task, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain group-level results.

This is an empirical event-related fMRI study of impression formation (perception/understanding of others), conducted in healthy adult participants (18–30 years, n=18 included). The paper reports group-level, random-effects, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (incongruent vs. congruent contrasts), with cluster-level results surviving FDR correction and coordinates presented in tables/figures. Thus it provides whole-brain healthy-group task activation maps relevant to social processing.

This fMRI study used a social-related task (viewing others performing body-checking and imagining oneself doing the actions), engaging self- and other-related/social-cognitive processing. It includes a healthy control group of adults (age-matched females; overall sample age range 17–34) and reports group-level, whole-brain task activation maps and coordinates for the healthy control group (figures and Table 2). Whole-brain analyses (voxelwise/cluster-level) are described and healthy-group activation is clearly reported. Therefore the study meets the review’s criteria for task domain (I3), healthy adult sample (I4), whole-brain healthy-group results (I5), and acceptable reporting of whole-brain results (I6).

The study uses task-based fMRI to investigate self-recognition (a social-cognition construct: Perception and Understanding of Self), with a healthy adult sample (n≈35, ages 18–24). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise random-effects analyses are reported (SPM5; contrasts, cluster- and voxel-level thresholds) with tables of coordinates and figures, satisfying whole-brain reporting. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-adult or clinical-only sample, or non-empirical) apply. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

The study reports fMRI activation to dynamic social interaction videos in a sample of 20 young adult volunteers (healthy adults). The task is explicitly social (positive and negative social encounters), satisfying the social-related task requirement. The abstract states whole-brain and hemispheric activation with significant right>left effects (p<0.0001) in multiple regions (amygdaloid complex, IFG, fusiform, temporal gyri), indicating group-level, whole-brain task-evoked results from the healthy sample. There is no indication that results are ROI-only, connectivity-only, or limited to non-adult ages. Full text access is limited, but the abstract provides clear evidence that inclusion criteria are met.

This study reports task-based fMRI in healthy adult participants (n=18, mean age 26) examining perception of different laughter types—a clear social-communication/social-cognition task. The paper presents group-level, voxelwise whole-brain analyses (conjunctions and contrasts) with coordinates and cluster results, and explicitly reports whole-brain and ROI-corrected results in tables/figures. Thus it meets all inclusion requirements for social-related fMRI in healthy adults and does not trigger any exclusion criteria.

This is an fMRI study of social-related processing (empathy/Theory of Mind) using verbal narratives to probe others’ physical and emotional pain. The sample comprises healthy adults (Narrative Experiment n=41, ages 18–37). The paper reports group-level whole-brain, voxelwise analyses (SnPM random-effects, corrected p<0.05) with contrasts and peak coordinates, and it uses functional localizers; whole-brain results are clearly described in the text and tables. Thus it meets the review’s requirements for task relevance, healthy adult sample, and reported whole-brain task activation maps.

This is an fMRI study using a social-related self-referential task (self, mother, president) meeting the review’s construct scope (Perception/Understanding of Self). It includes a healthy adult control group (n=15; ages 31–58) reported separately from the schizophrenia group. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise task activation maps for healthy controls (figures and whole-brain corrected results are presented and described), satisfying whole-brain evidence requirements. Results are reported as voxelwise contrasts and corrected maps/coordinates. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity/rest-only, between-group-only, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) are violated.

This is an fMRI study of social perception: participants viewed approaching characters making happy or angry expressions (social-related task assessing affiliation/dominance). Sample includes ten healthy young adult participants (healthy adults). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain random-effects voxelwise contrasts (Angry>Happy and Happy>Angry) with statistical thresholding, cluster coordinates, voxel counts, and figures—satisfying whole-brain task-evoked map reporting. Results for the healthy/control group are clearly presented. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, not between-group-only, participants are within adult range, and this is empirical fMRI data). Therefore all inclusion criteria are met.

This is an fMRI study of social-affective processing (mimicry, affiliation/appeasement) in healthy adults using a task manipulating emotion and group membership, satisfying the review topic. Sample: healthy adult participants (N=41 for fMRI analyses; ages reported, within 18–65). Whole-brain, group-level task activation contrasts are reported (e.g., Incongruent>Congruent and masked contrasts for Happy vs Angry, Out-group vs In-group) with cluster-level correction and tables of peak coordinates (Tables 2–4) and detailed methods for SPM analysis. Results are reported for the healthy/control group (no exclusive patient group). Whole-brain results are clearly described in text, tables, and figures. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6 and does not violate exclusion criteria (no ROI-only, resting-state-only, or non-empirical limitations).

This study uses fMRI during a social (multi-round trust game) task and includes a healthy adult control group (20 males, age 18–50), satisfying I3 and I4. However, the paper does not report an unmasked, whole-brain group-level task activation map for the healthy/control group. The only whole-brain analyses presented are exploratory voxel-wise between-group contrasts (control > patient), not a within-group healthy-task effect. Therefore it violates exclusion criterion E4 (only between-group contrasts without an accompanying unmasked healthy-group whole-brain task effect).

The study used fMRI during a social task (facial emotion recognition) in healthy adult participants; however, the paper reports whole-brain results only as between-group contrasts (LDA > HDA and HDA > LDA). It does not present an unmasked, group-level whole-brain task activation map (e.g., Emo_Emo > Neu_Age) clearly identified as coming from a healthy/control group independent of subgroup comparisons. Therefore it meets exclusion criterion E4 (only between-group contrasts without an accompanying whole-brain healthy-group task effect).

The study reports an fMRI experiment involving social-related processing (social reputation), meeting the review topic. The sample consists of 28 healthy young adult participants (14 male, 14 female; ages 20–24), satisfying the healthy adult sample criterion. The paper presents whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked activation analyses (thresholds, cluster-level FWE correction, peak voxels in MNI coordinates, and a results table), clearly identified as group-level results from the healthy/control sample. Whole-brain results are reported in text, figures, and a table of activations. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-healthy-only, or non-empirical) apply. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met.

The study is a proof-of-concept rt-fMRI/EEG neurofeedback correlation analysis targeting the right pSTS for social communication, but the manuscript reports correlations with a predefined ROI rather than reporting any group-level, whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical maps for a healthy adult group. No unmasked whole-brain healthy-group task activation map (voxelwise results or coordinate table of a whole-brain contrast) is described in the abstract/full text provided. Therefore it violates the requirement for whole-brain evidence and appears to present ROI-based analyses only.

This is an empirical fMRI study of social perception (directional head turns) using dynamic social stimuli and MVPA/univariate analyses. Participants are healthy adult volunteers (mean age 29, range 22–38), satisfying the sample criterion. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain (gray-matter–masked) analyses and corrected whole-volume results (FWE-corrected coordinates and maps) in the main and exploratory analyses, not limited to ROI-only results. Results for the healthy/control group are clearly described and reported (including tables/coordinates and figures). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, or out-of-range sample) apply. Therefore the study meets the inclusion criteria for the review.

The study used task-based fMRI to examine perception of emotional facial expressions (a social/affiliation-relevant process). The sample comprised 40 healthy volunteers (adults), and the paper reports group-level whole-brain task-evoked activations across multiple brain regions (thalamus, temporo-parietal regions, amygdala, cerebellum, cortical areas), indicating voxelwise whole-brain results rather than ROI-only analyses. Results are clearly described for the healthy/control group. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-adult sample, or non-empirical) apply. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met.

The provided full-text excerpt contains stimulus materials and the paper metadata (title, authors, journal) that strongly imply an fMRI study of social/irony processing. However, the excerpt does not include any methodological details: no participant demographics or ages to confirm a healthy adult sample (I4 cannot be verified), and no group-level, whole-brain task-evoked statistical maps or reported whole-brain results (I5/I6 cannot be verified). Because the review requires explicit reporting of a healthy adult group and whole-brain activation results, and these crucial elements are not present in the supplied content, the study cannot be confirmed to meet all inclusion criteria and must be excluded.

This study used task-based fMRI during face perception (socially relevant stimuli), includes a healthy adult control group (n=7, mean age 30 within 18–65), and reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (within-group deactivation maps for task vs. rest and group comparisons) with cluster-correction described. Healthy-control results are reported separately (within-group analysis and comparisons), not limited to ROI or connectivity-only approaches. Therefore it meets the review’s requirements for social-related fMRI in healthy adults and provides whole-brain task-evoked statistical maps or descriptions of them.

The study reports task-based fMRI during social evaluation (explicit approachability judgments of faces vs implicit sex judgment), directly addressing social-related processing. It describes group-level task contrasts showing activations (e.g., left amygdala, medial/middle/inferior frontal gyri) and BOLD correlations with trait anxiety, which indicates whole-brain task-evoked analyses were performed and reported. The sample is described as participants (healthy group) with trait anxiety measured, implying a healthy adult cohort. Thus it meets inclusion: I3 (fMRI social task), I4 (healthy adult participants reported), I5 (group-level whole-brain task activations reported), and I6 (results described in text/figures). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only contrasts, non-empirical) appear to apply based on the provided content.

This is an fMRI study of social cognition (action understanding) in healthy adults (N=19, ages 18–32). The task is social-related (why/how/what observation goals) and uses task-evoked, group-level voxelwise analyses. Although main analyses were restricted to an a priori mask of mirror neuron and mentalizing systems, the manuscript explicitly notes that details about the mask and whole-brain results are provided in the Supplemental Methods, and group-level random-effects analyses were conducted and reported (cluster coordinates/tables and figures). Thus it meets inclusion criteria for fMRI social task (I3), healthy adult sample (I4), whole-brain group-level voxelwise results (I5), and acceptability of coordinate/figure reporting (I6).

The study uses task-based fMRI to probe social-related processing (viewing and emotional evaluation of others’ faces—political candidates), meeting the review’s social processing scope. The sample consists of healthy adult participants (n=20; ages mean ~35) within the 18–65 range. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation maps and contrasts (faces vs rest; candidate pairwise contrasts; group comparisons), with thresholded Z maps, tables of coordinates, and figures—satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. Results are clearly from healthy adult groups and not limited to ROIs or connectivity-only analyses. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, resting-state-only, age out of range, non-empirical) are violated. Therefore the study should be included.

This fMRI study used a social-related task (explicit labeling of others’ brief emotional facial expressions), scanned healthy adult participants (N=50, ages 18–29), and reports whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked group-level contrasts and regression results (with cluster-level FWE correction) clearly identified for the healthy sample. Whole-brain results are reported in tables/figures and described in the text. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria and no exclusion criteria apply.

The study is an fMRI investigation of memory for emotional faces, which is a social-related task (perception and understanding of others). Participants are healthy adults (N=35, mean age 29). The paper reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses (random-effects ANCOVA, FDR<.05) with Talairach coordinates and whole-brain contrasts (emotion main effect, angry>neutral, load contrasts) clearly reported. Results are not limited to ROIs or connectivity-only analyses. Therefore it satisfies all inclusion criteria and violates none of the exclusion criteria.

The study reports task-based fMRI during social-related processing (facial emotion recognition and non-emotional face judgments), fulfilling social cognition construct. It includes a healthy adult control group (community controls aged 18–65) with results reported separately. The paper provides group-level, whole-brain task-evoked activation maps and between- and within-group whole-brain analyses (with tables and figures describing control within-group activations and contrasts), satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. Results for controls are clearly described in text, tables, and figures (including within-group activation maps and contrasts), meeting the reporting criterion. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not connectivity-only, includes healthy adults, is empirical). Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

The study used task-based fMRI probing social interaction (a social interaction simulation manipulating relationship type and valence), included a healthy adult sample (28 right-handed participants, age range 19–27), and reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (SPM5 random-effects; FWE- and cluster-corrected results, figures and Table 1 listing significant clusters). Healthy-group effects (main effects and interactions) are clearly described and reported. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, clinical-only samples) apply.
Screening failed:

The study reports task-based fMRI during incidental priming of participants’ own promotion/prevention goals — a social-cognitive/self-related processing task (fits social-related constructs such as Perception and Understanding of Self). The sample consists of 16 participants with no mention of clinical groups, indicating a healthy adult group is analyzed separately. The paper describes task-related cortical activation and identifies specific prefrontal regions associated with promotion goal priming and correlations with individual differences, consistent with reporting group-level whole-brain task-evoked activations rather than ROI-only or connectivity-only results. There is no indication of exclusionary issues (ROI-only analyses, connectivity-only, between-group-only effects, non-adult sample, or non-empirical paper). Confidence is moderated because the provided excerpt does not explicitly list participant ages or verbatim ‘whole-brain voxelwise’ terminology, but the reported cortical activations in a J. Cogn. Neurosci. empirical fMRI study support inclusion.

This is an fMRI study of social attribution (self-responsibility and self-serving bias) using task-based BOLD fMRI in healthy adult participants (12 neurologically healthy males, ages 20–51). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (SPM99; fixed-effects and follow-up random-effects ROI testing) with results presented as voxelwise statistical maps and coordinate tables. The task is clearly social-related (attribution of positive/negative social events). All inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This empirical fMRI study used a social cognition (virtual reality face-to-face) task and acquired whole-brain BOLD data. It included a healthy adult control group (n=14; ages matched to 18–45 sample) reported separately. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked contrasts for the healthy/control group (within-group Emotion vs Control maps, figures and tables of coordinates) using voxelwise thresholding. Reporting of coordinates and figures satisfies acceptable whole-brain result reporting. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity/resting-state only, between-group-only, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) apply. Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6 for the review.

This is an fMRI study of social-related processing using a pseudo-interactive joke task (action-outcome contingency), directly probing self/other social processing and reward. Sample: 38 healthy adult participants (ages 19–29) with analyses reported for the healthy group. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., SELF vs OTHER; action-outcome interaction) with cluster-level FWE correction, tables of coordinates, and figures—meeting whole-brain reporting requirements. Therefore all inclusion criteria are satisfied and no exclusion criteria are violated.

The study uses fMRI in healthy adult participants during a social-related task (audiovisual integration of non-verbal emotional signals) and reports group-level statistics for STS ROIs. However, the analysis is an ROI-based approach with parameter estimates extracted from individually mapped STS measuring points; the paper does not present an unmasked, whole-brain (voxelwise) group-level task activation map for the healthy/control group. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I5 and meets exclusion criterion E2 (ROI-only results).

This is an fMRI study of social/emotional processing (perception of fearful vs neutral body gestures), satisfying the social-related task requirement. The paper includes a healthy adult control group (adult males) reported separately and compared to the ASD group. The manuscript reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses for controls (contrasts, conjunction analyses, thresholded statistical maps, tables of coordinates and figures), providing the required whole-brain task-evoked results. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5 and I6. Confidence is high though exact control age range is not explicitly quoted in the excerpt; the text indicates adult controls and notes groups did not differ on age, supporting eligibility.

This is an event-related fMRI study of evaluative judgments (self-referential/social cognition/theory of mind), which is a social-related task. The paper includes a healthy adult control group (mean age ~26.4, within 18–65) reported separately. The authors present whole-brain, group-level task activation maps and coordinate tables for the control group (figures and Table 3) using voxelwise analyses corrected for multiple comparisons. Reporting includes within-group contrasts for controls (evaluative judgment vs. semantic retrieval), satisfying whole-brain evidence requirements. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is a longitudinal randomized fMRI study using the Ultimatum Game (a social economic exchange task) in healthy adult participants (N=51, ages ~31). The task probes social decision-making/trust/cooperation (social-related processing). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain, random-effects task-evoked analyses with voxelwise results (conjunction and interaction contrasts), corrected and uncorrected statistical maps, and coordinates reported in text/tables/supplementary material. Healthy/control group results are clearly described (pre- and post-training whole-brain effects for MT and CT groups). Thus it meets inclusion criteria for a whole-brain fMRI study of social processing in healthy adults.

The study reports a task-based fMRI investigation of social interaction and reactive aggression using an interactive Taylor paradigm (social perception/understanding of others). Participants were healthy adult males (N=16, mean age 28.6), satisfying the healthy adult sample requirement. Analyses used SPM2 with random-effects, whole-brain voxelwise statistics reported (thresholds, conjunctions, coordinates, activation maps and tables) for group-level task effects (retaliation, watching opponent, anticipation), and ROI splits by psychopathy are secondary; whole-brain healthy-group results are clearly presented. The paper therefore meets inclusion criteria for task-based social fMRI, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain group-level reporting (coordinates/figures). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only, out-of-range ages, or non-empirical) apply.

This paper reports an event-related fMRI study of perception of socially relevant facial expressions (social communication), i.e., a social-related task (I3). The sample comprises healthy adult participants (N=17, right-handed males, mean age 25.9) meeting the 18–65 criterion (I4). Group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (FIR model in SPM5) are reported with statistical parametric maps and MNI coordinates (random-effects inference; p=.001 uncorrected, extent threshold), satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements (I5,I6). The study is empirical and not ROI- or connectivity-only, and reports healthy-group task activations directly, so it meets inclusion criteria.

The study used task-based fMRI to measure brain responses during perception of biological motion, a social-related process (meets I3). It includes a healthy adult control group (n=15, mean age ~25), reported separately (meets I4). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain task activation maps/contrasts for the control group (biological motion vs scrambled) with coordinate tables and figures (meets I5 and I6). The analyses include whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (not limited to ROI-only or connectivity-only), and healthy-group effects are clearly presented, so no exclusion criteria are triggered. Therefore the study should be included.

The full text appears to be a brief conference abstract that does not report necessary methodological details. While the study describes fMRI during a social task (live eye contact) suggesting I3 is met, it does not provide participant details (number, ages, or clearly identified healthy adult group) to confirm I4, nor does it present or reference any group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task-evoked statistical maps (I5). Because the paper lacks reported healthy-group whole-brain task activation results, it fails the review’s required reporting standards and cannot be included.

Although the study uses task-based fMRI of a social stimulus (direct vs averted gaze) and includes a healthy adult control group (I3, I4), the paper reports only seed-based psychophysiological interaction (PPI) connectivity results rather than an unambiguous, whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked activation map for the healthy/control group. The reported whole-brain analyses refer to PPI (connectivity) contrasts and between-group connectivity comparisons; no healthy-group whole-brain task activation map (main effect or within-group task contrast of activation) is clearly presented. This matches exclusion criterion E3 (studies reporting only seed-based/effective connectivity without a healthy-group whole-brain task activation map). Therefore the study must be excluded from the meta-analysis.

This fMRI study used whole-brain, voxelwise analysis of BOLD responses while healthy adult participants (10 right-handed males, ages within 18–65) viewed funny vs. non-funny cartoons, a task involving social-cognitive processing (humor appreciation/social communication and understanding of others). Group-level whole-brain results are reported (Talairach coordinates, cluster statistics, p-values, table and figure), satisfying the reporting requirements. No exclusion criteria apply (not ROI-only, not resting-state, not between-group-only, and participants are healthy adults). Therefore all inclusion criteria are met.

This study employed task-based fMRI probing social-related processing (familiar/partner faces) relevant to affiliation/attachment and perception/understanding of others. It includes a healthy control group (n=13, mean age 64.5) reported separately from the patient, and presents group-level whole-brain voxelwise contrasts for the control group (partner > unfamiliar; FWE-corrected results and coordinates are reported). Results are described in figures/tables and whole-brain analyses are clearly attributed to the healthy/control group. The only minor uncertainty is that exact age ranges for controls are not listed (mean 64.5 ±5.7 suggests some participants may approach or slightly exceed 65), hence a confidence <1.0. Overall, the paper meets the review’s requirements for inclusion.

This is an event-related fMRI study of agency attribution (social cognition/Perception and Understanding of Others) using animated stimuli to evoke intentionality. Participants were healthy adults (n=12, mean age 25.2), within the 18–65 range. The paper reports group-level whole-brain, voxelwise random-effects analyses (contrasts High>Low and Low>High) with reported activated regions and statistical thresholds (p<0.001 uncorrected). Whole-brain task-evoked results are clearly described in the text and figures. Therefore the study meets all inclusion criteria for fMRI social processing in healthy adults and does not violate exclusion criteria.

This is an fMRI study of social communication processing in healthy adults (N=20, mean age 22). The task examines processing of communicative vs noncommunicative vocal sounds (social communication). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (vocal > nonvocal and communicative > noncommunicative) thresholded with FDR q<.05 and provides peak coordinates and whole-brain activation maps, satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. Therefore all inclusion criteria for the review are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This study used task-based fMRI to investigate vicarious somatosensory responses during observation of touch, which addresses social perception/understanding of others (social-related processing). The sample consisted of healthy adult participants (N=22, analyzed N=20; ages 23–39) meeting the age range. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain random-effects analyses with FWE-corrected results and coordinates (tables/figures) for the healthy participant group. Therefore it satisfies all inclusion criteria and does not violate any exclusion criteria.

This is an fMRI study that directly examines social-related processing (perception of others' eye gaze and social attention) using task-based functional MRI in healthy adult participants (n=9, mean age 24). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts to identify face-responsive regions (clusters selected with z>4 and cluster-size thresholds), and provides atlas coordinates and tables/figures of activations using SPM. Thus it meets criteria for using fMRI during a social task (I3), includes healthy adults in the 18–65 range (I4), reports whole-brain group-level task-evoked statistical maps (I5), and provides coordinates/figures as acceptable reporting (I6). No exclusion criteria apply.

This empirical fMRI study examines perception/understanding of others by comparing goal-directed (sports-related) versus non-goal-directed biological motion, a social-related task. Participants are healthy adults (mean age 29.4), and group-level whole-brain task contrasts (BR minus BU) are reported with voxelwise statistics and peak coordinates. Results include whole-brain corrected thresholds and uncorrected a priori ROIs, fulfilling reporting requirements. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-healthy sample, or non-empirical) apply.

This study is ineligible for the meta-analysis because it does not use task-based fMRI in healthy adults. It reports resting-state functional connectivity in a clinical sample (male adults with ASD) and examines effects of endogenous and exogenous oxytocin. There is no healthy/control group whole-brain task-evoked activation map: the MRI data are resting-state (intrinsic connectivity) rather than task-evoked, and results pertain to the ASD group; no separate healthy adult group results are reported. Therefore it matches the exclusion criterion for studies reporting only resting-state/seed-based connectivity without a healthy-group whole-brain task activation.

This is an fMRI experiment examining neural correlates of receiving empathic vs. unempathic social comments (social-related processing). The sample comprises healthy adults (n=20, mean age 26) with no neurological/psychiatric disorders. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (e.g., empathic>unempathic, negative>positive feedback) with cluster thresholds and FWE-corrected results and tables of activations. Reporting of whole-brain results in text/tables/figures meets acceptable reporting standards. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-healthy-only, etc.) apply. Therefore all inclusion criteria are satisfied.

This paper reports two fMRI experiments investigating understanding of intentions in social interaction, demonstrating anterior paracingulate cortex activation. The study addresses social-related processing (theory of mind/social interaction) using task-based fMRI in human participants and reports group-level activation (anterior PCC) consistent with whole-brain task effects. It was published in Journal of Cognitive Neuroscience (2004) and presents empirical fMRI results rather than a review. Therefore it meets the review objective and the inclusion criteria for fMRI social tasks, healthy adult sample reporting, and whole-brain results (reported as activation in anterior PCC). No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical) apply based on the available full-text abstract and bibliographic information.

The study uses fMRI during a social perception task and includes a healthy adult control group, but the full text reports whole-brain analyses only as between-group contrasts (patients vs. controls) and ROI follow-ups. The paper does not present an unmasked, whole-brain task activation map or group-level whole-brain contrast coming solely from the healthy/control group (e.g., a main effect or within-group HC contrast) that is clearly identified and reported. Therefore it violates exclusion criterion E4 (only between-group contrasts reported without an accompanying healthy-group whole-brain task effect).

The study uses task-based fMRI probing social reward (interpersonal pleasant touch) and reports behavioral and neural responses to social context. It includes a matched healthy control group of non-using adults and explicitly describes control-group neural activation (controls showed increased striatal activation to female vs male interaction), consistent with a group-level task effect. The abstract implies voxelwise whole-brain activation reporting (striatal activation differences) and whole-brain results are acceptable when presented in text/figures/tables. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, between-group-only without healthy-group map, non-adult sample, or non-empirical paper) appear to apply. Minor uncertainty remains because exact ages and the format of whole-brain results (tables/figures vs coordinates) are not shown in the abstract, hence confidence <1.0.

The study uses task-based fMRI during an explicit social task (imitate/observe emotional faces), includes a healthy adult group (ages 18–55) reported separately within the sample, and reports second-level, whole-brain group analyses (t-maps/contrast maps) derived from the task. The methods state that second-level analyses were run separately by site and group, and the manuscript presents whole-brain group-level maps and contrasts (e.g., imitate > observe) used in the clustering and group analyses. These whole-brain task-evoked results are clearly described and meet the reporting requirements. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, resting-state-only, out-of-age-range, or non-empirical) apply.

This is a task-based fMRI study of social processing (implicit interpersonal space/affiliation) in healthy adult participants (male, ages 19–30). The paper reports group-level whole-brain task-evoked analyses (main effects and interactions; random-effects GLM with cluster correction) and presents neuroimaging results in the text/figures, satisfying whole-brain reporting requirements. The sample is within the 18–65 range and results for the healthy group are reported. The study is empirical and not limited to ROI- or connectivity-only analyses. Therefore all inclusion criteria for the review are met and no exclusion criteria are triggered.

Although this fMRI study used a social-related simulation task (empathy for pain) and included a healthy adult control group reported separately (satisfying I3 and I4), the paper does not provide an unmasked, group-level whole-brain task activation map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group alone. Whole-brain results are reported for the full sample (HC + SZ) and no HC-only whole-brain contrasts/maps are presented. Primary neuroimaging inferences rely on ROI analyses and combined-group whole-brain ANOVA; thus the study lacks the required healthy-group whole-brain task-evoked map. This violates exclusion criterion E4 (no accompanying unmasked, whole-brain healthy-group task effect).

The study used fMRI during a social-related task (facial emotion processing) and reports group-level whole-brain task activation analyses for the healthy control group (paired t-tests, one-sample t-tests; threshold p<0.05 FWE corrected). Healthy control results are reported separately from the clinical group. Although the sample age range includes 16–40 years (so some participants may be under 18), the healthy group is reported as a distinct control group within the adult range (up to 40). Thus the paper meets the review’s criteria for fMRI social-task, healthy adult controls, and whole-brain healthy-group results; confidence tempered slightly by the reported lower bound of the overall sample age range.

This is an fMRI study using a social cognition task (theory of mind and empathy cartoon task), conducted in healthy adult participants (N=13, ages 19–36). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain, voxelwise task-evoked contrasts analyzed with SPM2 (random-effects) and presents significant activation foci (thresholds, clusters, and tables/figures). Whole-brain results for the healthy/control group are clearly described. Therefore it satisfies the review inclusion criteria for an fMRI social-related task in healthy adults and provides whole-brain group-level results.

This study reports fMRI of social cognition using a validated, naturalistic Theory of Mind task (MASC), satisfying the social-related task requirement. The sample comprises healthy adults (n=18, age range 20–45), meeting the sample criterion. The paper presents group-level, whole-brain task-evoked activation results (GLM contrasts ToM vs PI) with thresholding, cluster correction, and tabulated coordinates and figures, fulfilling whole-brain reporting requirements. Results for the healthy/control sample are clearly reported. No exclusion criteria are triggered (not ROI-only, not resting-state/only connectivity, and not a non-empirical paper). Therefore the study meets inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6.

Although the study uses fMRI during face processing (a social-related task), the sample consists entirely of individuals with chronic traumatic brain injury (no healthy adult/control group reported separately). Therefore it does not meet inclusion criterion I4 (at least one healthy adult group). Because no unmasked, whole-brain healthy-group task activation map is provided, it fails the review’s requirement for healthy-group whole-brain results. Exclusion is based on the absence of a healthy adult whole-brain task effect.

The study reports functional MRI during a social cognition task in which participants repeatedly inferred others’ emotions and received feedback—clearly a social-related task. The abstract indicates participants were scanned (perceivers) and no clinical/special groups are mentioned, implying a healthy adult sample. The paper reports trial-by-trial learning signals that tracked activity in ventral striatum, ventromedial PFC, and TPJ, which indicates voxelwise whole-brain task-evoked results were analyzed and reported. Reporting in J Cogn Neurosci further supports standard whole-brain analyses. Although the abstract does not state exact ages, the sample is described as typical adult perceivers with no clinical exclusion; thus inclusion criteria I3, I4, I5, and I6 are satisfied.

The study used fMRI during a social cognitive (Theory-of-Mind) task but the sample comprises only clinical participants (schizophrenia and schizoaffective disorder) with no healthy adult control group and no reported whole-brain task activation map for a healthy/control group. Therefore it does not meet the requirement for inclusion of a healthy adult group (I4) nor provides a healthy-group whole-brain task effect (I5). This violates the review’s eligibility criteria for healthy-group whole-brain task maps. Exclusion applied: E4.

This study used task-based fMRI during social judgement tasks (approachability/intelligence) in healthy adult participants, reporting separate healthy control group results. Group-level whole-brain voxelwise contrasts (social > gender) for healthy males and females are reported, with peak coordinates, thresholding, and figures/tables described. Thus it meets I3 (fMRI social task), I4 (healthy adult group reported separately), I5 (whole-brain group-level voxelwise maps reported), and I6 (results presented in figures/coordinates). No exclusion criteria are violated.

This study used task-based fMRI to examine human perception of affective vocalisations (social communication/perception of others), matching the review’s social-related constructs. Sample: healthy adult participants (N=19, mean age 25.9) within the 18–65 range. Whole-brain, group-level voxelwise task contrasts are reported (e.g., species contrast human > chimpanzee > macaque) with MNI coordinates, tables and figures (p < .001 uncorrected), fulfilling the requirement for whole-brain evidence. Results for the healthy/control group are clearly reported. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an fMRI study using a social judgment task (dominance/trustworthiness of faces) in healthy adults (N=23, ages 21–43). The paper reports whole-brain, group-level task activation maps and provides voxelwise results with a table of peak coordinates and cluster-level FWE-corrected results for the Social Judgment > Perceptual Judgment contrast. Results for the healthy adult group are clearly reported. Therefore it meets all required inclusion criteria and violates no exclusion criteria.

This is an event-related fMRI study of facial emotion processing (social perception/understanding of others), involving an implicit social task. It includes a healthy adult control group (n=9, mean age 27±5) reported separately. The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise activation maps and analyses for the control group (figures, tables, and supplementary materials) using voxel- and cluster-wise thresholding. Reporting of whole-brain results in tables/figures satisfies acceptable formats. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity/resting-state-only, only between-group without healthy-group maps, age outside 18–65, or non-empirical) apply. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

This paper is a tutorial/methods/review article about intersubject correlation (ISC) analysis and related techniques. It does not report original empirical fMRI data from participants, does not describe a specific social-task experiment with a healthy adult sample, and does not present any group-level, whole-brain task activation maps for a healthy/control group. Therefore it does not meet the inclusion criteria requiring original fMRI task data and whole-brain results. Excluded under E6 (non-empirical paper without original fMRI data in healthy adults).

The study exclusively reports data from patients with bipolar disorder (no healthy control group is included or reported). Although it uses whole-brain fMRI during a social-related task (facial emotion/gender discrimination), it does not provide any group-level whole-brain task-evoked map for a healthy adult sample. Therefore it fails inclusion criterion I4 (healthy adult group) and must be excluded under E4 (no accompanying unmasked whole-brain healthy-group task effect).

This is an empirical fMRI study of social communication (L2 communication vs description), directly addressing social-related processing. The sample comprises 30 healthy adult native Japanese speakers (L2 learners), satisfying the healthy adult sample requirement. The paper reports group-level brain activations (e.g., left posterior supramarginal gyrus, left MTG, OFC/insula) clearly described as task-evoked effects for the healthy participant group, indicating whole-brain voxelwise results (reported in text/figures/tables). Reporting meets the allowance for coordinate/figure/table presentation. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-empirical, out-of-range ages, or only between-group contrasts) appear to apply. Therefore all required inclusion criteria are met.

This fMRI study investigates third-party punishment, a social cognitive task involving mentalizing and judgment about others (social processing). It reports data from 26 healthy adult participants (mean age 26) within the 18–65 range. The authors performed whole-brain, group-level GLM analyses and report whole-brain task-evoked activations (Decision Phase: Experimental > Control) with FDR-corrected thresholds and coordinate tables/figures, satisfying the requirement for whole-brain evidence. Results are clearly described for the healthy group. No exclusion criteria apply.

This is an fMRI study in healthy adult participants (N=25, mean age 25.7) that explicitly probes social-related processing (guilt, social cognition, perspective-taking). The methods report group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., guilt memories vs neutral memories) with whole-brain thresholding (p<0.001, cluster extent) and report coordinates/regions; results are presented for the healthy sample. The task involves social scenarios and personal recollections relevant to perception/understanding of others/self. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-adult sample, or non-empirical) apply. Thus it meets all required inclusion criteria for the review.

This is an empirical fMRI study using the Ultimatum Game (a social decision-making task) and reports whole-brain, group-level task contrasts. The sample includes a healthy adult group (young adults age 19–28) with results for that group reported separately. The paper provides voxelwise contrasts (unfair–fair) and group-level statistical maps/tables for the adult group. Reporting of whole-brain results is in figures/tables and described in text. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria for the review.

Although this is an fMRI study of audiovisual speech (a form of social communication) including a healthy adult control group, the paper does not present a whole-brain, group-level task activation map clearly identified as coming from the healthy/control group alone. The reported whole-brain main effect of audiovisual congruency is across combined participants and the paper focuses on group-by-congruency interactions; no unmasked, healthy-group whole-brain task contrast (or map) is reported. This violates the requirement for healthy-group whole-brain task-evoked results. Inclusion criteria I3 and I4 are met, but exclusion criterion E4 applies.

This is an empirical fMRI study investigating neural responses to witnessing emergencies (bystander effect) using task-evoked BOLD contrasts. Participants were healthy adults (ages 18–27). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise analyses (random-effects GLM, parametric and contrast maps) with results presented in tables and figures. The task is a social-related paradigm probing perception/understanding of others and action preparation in a bystander context. No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-healthy-only groups, or non-empirical) apply. Therefore the study meets all inclusion requirements for the review objective.

While the study is an fMRI investigation of social gaze processing in a sample of healthy adult participants (meets the review aim and sample criteria), all reported neuroimaging results are ROI-based (amygdala and inferior occipital gyrus) with statistical inference reported FWE-corrected within those ROIs. The paper does not present or describe an unmasked, group-level whole-brain (voxelwise) task-evoked statistical map or whole-brain coordinate tables for the healthy/control group. Therefore it fails the requirement for whole-brain evidence and meets exclusion criterion E2 (ROI-only results).

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants (N=22, mean age 21.6) investigating social cognition (emotion identification and attribution — perception and understanding of others). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., How>Why, Why>How) with FDR-corrected statistical maps and tables of coordinates. Whole-brain results for the healthy/control group are clearly presented. Therefore it meets all inclusion criteria and none of the exclusion criteria.

This is an empirical fMRI study of social-related processing (perception of biological motion/social stimuli) in healthy adult participants (final N=26; ages 18–39). The paper reports both ROI analyses and whole-brain, voxelwise analyses: a whole-brain analysis of biological-motion selectivity and social-network measures yielded a significant cluster in the right pSTS (reported in text and supplemental Figure S1) with correction for multiple comparisons. Whole-brain results are clearly described for the healthy group. Therefore all relevant inclusion criteria are met.

This study reports task-based fMRI of social-related touch (self vs other touch), which directly addresses social perception and self/other processing. It includes a healthy adult control group (n=30; ages within 18–65) and reports group-level, whole-brain task-evoked activation maps for the neurotypical controls (e.g., “Other-touch in NC” and self-touch contrasts reported at whole-brain FWE-corrected thresholds). Results for the control group are presented separately and whole-brain effects are clearly described in text and figures. The paper is empirical and uses task-based fMRI rather than only ROI-only or connectivity-only analyses. Therefore it satisfies inclusion criteria I3 (fMRI social-related task), I4 (healthy adult sample reported separately), I5 (group-level whole-brain task maps), and I6 (whole-brain results clearly described). No exclusion criteria are met.

This is an empirical fMRI study in healthy adult participants (three cultural groups, n=78, ages within 18–65) that used a social cognition task (reading personal narratives involving others and moral/protected values). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task contrasts (e.g., stories vs rest; protected-value stories vs non-protected) with cluster correction and describes whole-brain results in the text and figures. Thus it meets the fMRI social task requirement, healthy adult sample, and whole-brain reporting (including coordinates/figures). No exclusion criteria (ROI-only, connectivity-only, non-healthy-only, or non-empirical) are violated.

This publication is a review article (non-empirical) and does not report original fMRI data, participant samples, methods, or any group-level whole-brain task-evoked statistical maps from healthy adults. It therefore does not meet the requirement for original fMRI results in healthy adults and should be excluded.

This empirical fMRI study includes a social decision-making (altruism) task probing perceptions of others’ outcomes and focus on a partner’s feelings – clearly a social-related construct. Participants are healthy adults (altruism N=55, subset N=37 also did food task; mean age ~28, within 18–65). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain multivariate searchlight decoding results and cluster coordinates (conjunctions, voxelwise maps, and ROI analyses) showing task-evoked effects; statistical thresholds and MNI coordinates are provided and derived maps are available on OSF. Thus it provides whole-brain, healthy-group task activation/decoding maps relevant to social processing. No exclusion criteria (e.g., ROI-only, resting-state only, non-healthy or out-of-range sample) apply.

This is an fMRI study of social perception (animacy, action observation, theory-of-mind related processes) in healthy adult participants (final N=23, mean age 26.4). The task is social-related (perception and understanding of others), and the paper reports group-level whole-brain, voxelwise task activation analyses (voxel-wise threshold p<0.005, cluster correction; peak coordinates and clusters are listed). Results for main effects and interactions are clearly described for the healthy/control group. Therefore it meets inclusion criteria for functional MRI social-task data with whole-brain results.

The study uses fMRI in healthy adults and reports whole-brain task-evoked analyses (coordinates and cluster-corrected maps) and includes a healthy adult group (younger group age 19–28), satisfying I4, I5, and I6. However, the experimental task is a word/pseudoword repetition task focused on speech production and motor/phonological processes rather than a social-processing or social-communication task. Although the introduction discusses social aspects of imitation, the task itself does not involve social interaction, affiliation/attachment, perception of others, or explicit social communication paradigms. Therefore it does not meet the required social-related task inclusion criterion (I3) and must be excluded.

This study reports task-based fMRI of social processing (fearful faces with gaze manipulation), includes a clearly defined healthy adult control group (n=22, ages within 18–65) with results reported separately, and presents group-level whole-brain voxelwise analyses (within-group contrasts for controls and between-group comparisons) with corrected statistical maps. Thus it meets the meta-analysis requirements for social-related fMRI in healthy adults.

This is an fMRI task study probing social auditory processing (listening to one vs. two walkers), clearly addressing social-related processing. The sample comprises healthy adults (n=12; ages 22–37). The paper reports group-level whole-brain voxelwise GLM results and statistical maps/coordinate tables for contrasts (e.g., STEP1+STEP2 – REST; STEP1 – NOISE1; STEP2 – NOISE2), normalized to Talairach space. Whole-brain contrasts and coordinates are explicitly described for the healthy participant group, satisfying whole-brain evidence requirements. The study is empirical, not ROI-only, not resting-state, and includes direct task-evoked activations. Therefore all inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This is an empirical task-based fMRI study of social processing (attentional orienting to eye gaze vs arrows with social voice vs tone contexts) in healthy adults (n=22, mean age ~23). The paper reports group-level, whole-brain voxelwise task activation analyses (main effects and interactions) with appropriate statistical thresholds and tables/figures, and also provides ROI/small-volume correction results. All relevant inclusion criteria are met and no exclusion criteria apply.

This fMRI study directly investigates social communication (communicative vs. descriptive speech) in healthy adult participants (native Japanese, ages 19–31).
